title: Ravens’ 2026 season has come to a crashing halt
summary: It took just one play. As optimistically as it began, the 2026 Ravens season is all but finished. On the first day of November, on his first snap back from a high-ankle sprain, Lamar Jackson injured his right thumb when his throwing hand struck the wrist of Bills pass rusher Greg Rousseau. Jackson knew something […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 1: Trainers attend to Lamar Jackson #8 of the Baltimore Ravens kneels after getting hurt on the first play of the game against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images It took just one play. As optimistically as it began, the 2026 Ravens season is all but finished. On the first day of November, on his first snap back from a high-ankle sprain, Lamar Jackson injured his right thumb when his throwing hand struck the wrist of Bills pass rusher Greg Rousseau. Jackson knew something was wrong immediately, sprinting straight to the sideline and then to the locker room. The two-time MVP has since had surgery on his thumb with a late-season return technically in play – if it even matters. At this point, Jackson is the Baltimore Ravens, and his contract reflects that. Many want to bash the supporting cast, the coaches and the front office, but it just isn’t realistic for a team paying a star quarterback that much to also have stars at every other position. What did the Chiefs look like without Patrick Mahomes last year? What did the Bengals look like without Joe Burrow? What would the Bills look like without Josh Allen? On top of losing Jackson, the Ravens have suffered a rash of injuries elsewhere, primarily on the offensive line. A position group that typically thrives on continuity is operating with a new offensive coordinator, a new offensive line coach, and a rotating door of new starters. This year, the unit has had five different centers and four different right guards. Has the offensive line been good enough? No. But we never got to see the vision. Heck, we never even got to see Jackson and Zay Flowers play a full game together. The full extent of the Ravens’ woes came to a head five days after the Jacksonville Jaguars. With undrafted rookie quarterback Joe Fagnano making his first start, the Ravens were once again trounced at home, this time in a downpour. We all expected the offense to struggle, and predictably, it did. But once again, the defense let the dam break. Is that partly a product of the offense’s struggles? Probably. Still, it looked more like a group of unmotivated, aging players struggling to adjust to a new defensive system. Marlon Humphrey and Malaki Starks were both burned for big plays, and the middle of the field — an area that has plagued this defense for years — was wide open all night for Trevor Lawrence. And yet, Monday night’s loss to the Chargers might have been worse. Jacoby Brissett performed admirable in his Ravens debut, but an anemic running game and a defense that once again could not tackle gifted a winless team their first victory. Unfortunately, the near future doesn’t look much brighter, largely because of some questionable decisions by the front office. The Ravens’ so-called “star” veterans by salary have underperformed this year. Marlon Humphrey, Roquan Smith, Ronnie Stanley, Mark Andrews and John Simpson make up more than 25% of the Ravens’ salary cap. That’s not a winning formula. It’s easy to engage in revisionist history on contracts. Humphrey signed his extension in 2020 and Smith signed his in early 2023. Since then, both have followed the natural arc of an NFL second contract: some very good years, and now the back end of their careers. Humphrey was an All-Pro in 2024, and Smith was an All-Pro in 2022 and 2023. Their decline isn’t surprising. What’s surprising is that the Ravens have forgotten one of Ozzie Newsome’s favorite phrases: ‘better to move on from a player a year too early rather than a year too late.’ It might be two years late for Humphrey now. Smith’s decision point should be this offseason. His oversized contract is arguably worse. Fred Warner is probably the only middle linebacker in the NFL worth that kind of money. Humphrey has virtually seen himself out the door in the last week; if the Ravens are committed to change, Smith should be gone this offseason, too. Now let’s talk about Mark Andrews. In my opinion, re-signing him was the worst contract DeCosta has ever handed out. Andrews has been terrible. So bad that he’s actively hurting the team. From 2019 to 2025, the Ravens consistently had one of the best tight end rooms in the league. Now it’s one of the worst. Meanwhile, as many of us suspected he would, Isaiah Likely is looking like one of the best tight ends in football. For his entire tenure in Baltimore, we assumed he’d be Andrews’ successor. That said, I don’t think it’s fair to claim the Ravens have simply punted on the trenches. On defense, Trey Hendrickson, Nnamdi Madubuike and Travis Jones all got paid. On the offensive line, the Ravens re-signed Ronnie Stanley, traded picks for center Cam Jurgens, spent their 2026 first-round pick on a guard and drafted Roger Rosengarten in the second round. The problem is that those players aren’t playing up to their price. Stanley and Rosengarten are both playing like average tackles. On the interior, Jurgens has been fine, but he hasn’t looked like he is worth a second-round pick. John Simpson hasn’t been much better than what the Ravens had at guard last year, though he’s dealt with a groin injury for most of the season. The Ravens trust their development process to a fault. Sometimes it’s paid off, but there have been far too many instances where it hasn’t, especially on the offensive line. Emery Jones Jr., Andrew Vorhees and Daniel Faalele have been abject developmental failures. Some of it is just bad luck. Ronnie Stanley was one of the best tackles in the NFL before his gruesome ankle injury. Since then, he’s played just well enough to earn another contract. But that’s the issue: the Ravens have been fine with “just good enough.” Rather than proactively building a dominant offensive line, they’ve settled for adequate. Look at the elite teams in the NFL right now. The Bills, 49ers, Lions, Bears, Broncos and even the Steelers all have top offensive lines. Obviously, if it were that easy, every team would do it. But when you have a superstar quarterback, protecting him is paramount. In a way, the 2024 season did them in. Despite two below-average guards, the Ravens put together a record-setting offense, so naturally, DeCosta thought it prudent to run it back. Let’s face it: when Jackson is healthy, the Ravens have typically had great offenses regardless of who’s blocking for him. Even this year, the Ravens ranked second in EPA per play with Jackson and this current group.The downside is that when Jackson is injured or hobbled, the team falls apart because the line can’t impose its will on opponents. If the Ravens are serious about building a championship team, they need to pour as many resources as possible into the trenches. Teams don’t fear playing the Ravens anymore because they’ve become largely a finesse team, with undersized corners, offensive linemen, linebackers and receivers. As a result, they can’t salt away games like they used to. In the second half, when opponents know the run is coming, the Ravens get shut down. Their status as one of the league’s worst short-yardage teams reflects that.In the early stages of the Lamar Jackson era, the major question was whether the Ravens could play from behind. They were that good at putting opponents away. Now it’s the opposite. DeCosta also has a habit of overcorrecting for past problems. The Ravens struggled to draft and develop receivers, so he spent multiple first-round picks trying to find one instead of trading for an established star, the way the team did with Anquan Boldin. The Ravens went through a few years where they couldn’t keep cornerbacks healthy, so he overcorrected again, spending pick after pick on corners to make sure it wouldn’t happen again. The better approach: trade for stars at the positions you’ve historically failed to develop. DeCosta also has a habit of being too loyal to his players. In one of his first press conferences as…

title: 3 Keys to Victory for Ravens-Panthers in Week 11
summary: This is it. You can’t finish with a record of 11-6 until you first reach 5-6. Technically, the Ravens could make the playoffs with seven or eight losses — but this feels like a defining moment. With the Houston Texans on the rise, Tampa Bay’s roster built perfectly to beat the Ravens, and then four […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 16: Mike Green #15 of the Baltimore Ravens celebrates during an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Chargers at M&T Bank Stadium on November 16, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images This is it. You can’t finish with a record of 11-6 until you first reach 5-6. Technically, the Ravens could make the playoffs with seven or eight losses — but this feels like a defining moment. With the Houston Texans on the rise, Tampa Bay’s roster built perfectly to beat the Ravens, and then four division games in a row, this game against Carolina feels like the easiest one remaining on the schedule. If the Ravens lose, any little fleeting hope for a run will fizzle. It’s been a drama-filled week for the Ravens, and they’ll be missing Nnamdi Madubuike, so they need to figure out how to put their heads down and grind out this win to avoid dropping six in a row. Find the formation that works The Ravens have run multiple tight end sets at the seventh-highest rate this year, 43.6% of the time, according to Next Gen Stats. They are largely successful throwing out of these sets as well, averaging 8.1 yards per pass attempt, which is 12th-most in the league. The issue is they pass out of 12 and 13 personnel less than 40% of the time, according to SumerSports. This both inflates their pass success rate and shows they are running more than 60% of the time out of these formations, allowing defenses to key in on the run. Recently, Declan Doyle has had an issue with running out of heavy on first down too frequently, making it very obvious and setting the Ravens behind the chains. The Ravens need to start mixing it up more. That could mean throwing out of heavy on early downs more often to catch the Panthers by surprise. The biggest issue there is that the Panthers have allowed the third-fewest yards per attempt against multi-tight end sets (5.8). The real solution might just be to lean on Jacoby Brissetts arm, play more 11 personnel, and sling the ball around the field to Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman and Ja’Kobi Lane. The Panthers have been down their top three cornerbacks for a while. Rookie Will Lee is expected to return in this one, but Jaycee Horn remains on IR and Mike Jackson, while practicing this week, hasn’t been activated yet. The Ravens might want to test whoever is covering their wide receivers. Spreading the offense out in 11 might help the run game as well if the Ravens can find success early through the air and back the Panthers off the line of scrimmage and out of the box. Finishes from Mike Green and Trey Hendrickson Hendrickson leads the Ravens in pressures despite missing two games and dealing with a figure injury since Week 1. He’s also getting double-teamed 42% of his pass rush snaps, according to ESPN. He also only has two sacks through his first eight games as a Raven, and that simply isn’t good enough or what the Ravens paid for. Conversely, the Ravens have seen Green get better throughout this season while going through some ups and downs, switching from one side of the defensive front to the other. He leads the Ravens in sacks with 5.5. The Panthers’ biggest overall weakness is their offensive line. Both of Carolina’s offensive tackles have been question marks this season. Their rookie right tackle, Monroe Freeling, has a 6-foot-7 frame with speed and athleticism, but the transition from left tackle in college to right in the NFL hasn’t been without questions. Rasheed Walker on the left side has struggled this season and given up a chunk of sacks as well. Without Madubuike, the Ravens need their two top edge rushers to get pressures and, more importantly, finish. Middle of the field defense It’s no surprise to anyone who watches Ravens games that their defense has given up a lot over the middle of the field. They’ve also been the worst defense on intermediate passes, giving up a league-worst 0.77 EPA per play on passes between 10 and 19 yards. Furthermore, the Ravens have been targeted on in-breaking routes on 36.7% of opponents’ passes, giving up seven touchdowns on them, 10th most in the league according to Next-Gen Stats. Meanwhile, the Panthers have four different 6-foot-4 wide receivers, and Bryce Young has thrown in-breakers on 38.8% of his routes, averaging 9.0 yards per attempt on these routes. That’s a lot of size and a lot of attempts for Roquan Smith to cover over the middle. Jesse Minter’s defense is designed to leave the middle of the field open; it’s the hardest area of the field to consistently throw in, with the most bodies, hands, arms, and heads to navigate. The idea is to funnel passes there, force as many tough throws as possible, and then have 11 hats on the ball to tackle quickly when passes do get caught there. It hasn’t worked so far. The Ravens players haven’t executed it consistently all season, and Minter has yet to deviate from it. Something has to change, and this would be a great game to make changes for it.

Thompson, 32, played in 12 regular-season games for Buffalo last season, starting 6. He totaled 56 tackles, 1 sack, 6 tackles for loss, 2 pass breakups, […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - JANUARY 17: Tre'Davious White #27 of the Buffalo Bills looks on from the field during an NFL divisional playoff football game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on January 17, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Grappling with injuries on defense, the Buffalo Bills have elevated linebacker Shaq Thompson and cornerback Tre’Davious White from their practice squad ahead of Sunday’s matchup with the Miami Dolphins. The Bills have elevated ILB Shaq Thompson and CB Tre'Davious White from the practice squad for tomorrow’s game. — Sal Capaccio 🏈 (@SalSports) November 21, 2026 Thompson, 32, played in 12 regular-season games for Buffalo last season, starting 6. He totaled 56 tackles, 1 sack, 6 tackles for loss, 2 pass breakups, and 1 fumble recovery. In Buffalo’s two playoff games, Thompson was excellent, notching 13 total tackles, a team-high 10 solo tackles, 2 tackles for loss, and an interception. The veteran is a former first-round pick of the Carolina Panthers, having been the No. 25 overall selection in the 2015 NFL Draft. Thompson will have a role this week in place of Dorian Williams, who is out with a calf injury that he suffered late in last week’s win over the New York Jets. Whether Thompson plays a significant role on defense or not is yet to be determined, but at worst, he provides strong depth for the Bills. Rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr is the other likely option to start next to Terrel Bernard. White, 31, also spent last season with the Bills. He played a significant part in the team’s defense, starting 16 games in the regular season across from Christian Benford. It’s thanks to Benford’s injured groin that White finds himself elevated this week, as he’ll either start across from rookie Davison Igbinosun or serve as depth behind the second-year man that he started over last season, Maxwell Hairston. During the 2025 season, White totaled 40 tackles, 10 pass breakups, and an interception. In the postseason, White started both games, totaling six tackles and three pass breakups. White originally entered the NFL in 2017 as Buffalo’s first-round draft choice that year, and after spending the 2024 season with the Baltimore Ravens and Los Angeles Rams, he returned home and played well last season. White allowed just 51% of the pass thrown when he was the closest man in coverage to be completed, holding opposing quarterbacks to a 71.1 quarterback rating when targeting him. The Bills and Dolphins are a 1 p.m. EDT start on Sunday. Each team’s official inactive lists will be released 90 minutes prior to kickoff.

A surprise report originating from the team on Saturday afternoon revealed that Bills starting defensive tackle Ed Oliver is dealing with an oblique injury. Oliver is now listed as questionable for Sunday’s home game, though […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 1: Ed Oliver #91 of the Buffalo Bills reacts as he takes the field against the Baltimore Ravens prior to an NFL football game at Highmark Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The injuries continue piling up for the Buffalo Bills ahead of their Week 11 home game against the Miami Dolphins. A surprise report originating from the team on Saturday afternoon revealed that Bills starting defensive tackle Ed Oliver is dealing with an oblique injury. Oliver is now listed as questionable for Sunday’s home game, though the news is not all doom and gloom. Matt Parrino provided some context to Oliver’s injury , tweeting that “(p)er a league source, Ed Oliver notified Bills training staff this morning that he felt pain in his oblique. The staff checked it out and there’s optimism that he’ll play against the Dolphins.” Per NFL rules, Oliver’s ailment must be accounted for on the injury report even at this late stage, which is why he’s being listed as questionable. In the past, Oliver’s situation would have likely had him tabbed as “probable” for game day. The NFL has since done away with that injury designation, which has seen the questionable term pick up the slack in filing injuries throughout the league. Should Oliver be unable to go (or limited in some fashion) it would be a huge blow to Buffalo’s defense, which already has to account for injuries to starters in cornerback Christian Benford and inside linebacker Dorian Williams. Both Bills defenders have been ruled out ahead of Week 11 .

title: 5 Miami Dolphins to watch at the Buffalo Bills
summary: The Buffalo Bills host the Miami Dolphins on Sunday in a game of two franchises headed in completely opposite directions. The 8-1 Bills sit atop the AFC, leading the conference by one game over the Jacksonville Jaguars and Kansas City Chiefs (the Denver Broncos are also 7-2, but they are currently the No. 5 seed […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills host the Miami Dolphins on Sunday in a game of two franchises headed in completely opposite directions. The 8-1 Bills sit atop the AFC, leading the conference by one game over the Jacksonville Jaguars and Kansas City Chiefs (the Denver Broncos are also 7-2, but they are currently the No. 5 seed in the playoff picture). Miami, on the other hand, is 1-8 and tied for the AFC’s worst record with the Los Angeles Chargers and Tennessee Titans. On paper, this a game that Buffalo should win running away. However, games are played on the field, not on paper, and Miami has kept plenty of games close this season. Half of Miami’s losses have come in one-possession games, and they’ve held great offenses like the Chiefs and the Detroit Lions under their season scoring average. If the Bills want to avoid the pitfalls of a textbook “trap game,” they’ll need to lock in and focus on stopping Miami’s key players. Here are five Dolphins to watch in Sunday’s tilt with the Bills. _____________________________________________________________________________ RB Ollie Gordon After De’Von Achane went down with a knee injury earlier this season, it was easy to assume that Miami’s run game would suffer mightily. Thanks to Gordon, though, Miami has been able to run fairly well throughout the course of the year. With former Syracuse Orange quarterback Kyle McCord set to make his second career start this week, Miami will want to try to establish the run and maintain possession of the ball to keep their young quarterback out of obvious passing situations. Shutting Gordon down and keeping Miami in continuous second-and-long or third-and-long scenarios will go a long way towards driving the Bills to victory this week. Buffalo has been good against the run, as they are No. 8 in yards allowed on the ground. Gordon averages 4.2 yards per rush. If the Bills can prevent him from breaking big runs, they’ll be in great shape. WR Malik Washington Buffalo’s secondary is beaten up, and while the Dolphins don’t boast a great passing attack, they do have some sneaky-good weapons who can beat you if you aren’t careful. Chief among those weapons is Washington, who leads Miami in targets (51), receptions (36), and receiving yards (400). At 5’8” and 192 lbs., he operates out of the slot more often than not, so it will be up to whomever Buffalo plays inside to contain him. Given their injuries in the secondary, that responsibility could fall to Dee Alford, Jordan Hancock, Damar Hamlin, or a combination of multiple defenders, including linebackers. Washington is particularly good after the catch, as 123 of his 400 receiving yards have come as “YAC” gains. If he catches a short pass, that’s fine; what the Bills can’t do is let him slip tackles and pick up big gains after he makes that grab. DE Chop Robinson The 2024 first-round pick is on pace for a career year, and good for him. It took Robinson some time to put it together as a pro, but he has five sacks already on the season, which is one shy of the career-high six sacks he notched as a rookie. He also has 13 quarterback hits, which is just one shy of his career-high total from that same 2024 rookie season. Both Spencer Brown and Dion Dawkins are likely to play this week, so Buffalo should finally be back at full strength along the offensive line after playing some different combinations due to injury over the last three weeks. Making sure that Robinson stays out of the offensive backfield needs to be a major focus of the game plan. LB Jacob Rodriguez While the Rookie of the Year hype that came with Rodriguez in the season’s early going has faded a bit, what hasn’t faded is the quality of Rodriguez’s play. The rookie out of Texas Tech has looked every bit the part of a long-term starter at middle linebacker for a Miami defense that has played better than the team’s 1-8 record would suggest. Rodriguez was a fan favorite for many Bills-connected folks during the draft process last spring, and his play so far has justified that hype. He has 80 tackles, four tackles for loss, one sack, one interception, and one forced fumble so far this season. Head coach and offensive playcaller Joe Brady needs to try to give the rookie some different looks by using motion to throw off his keys. That should help Buffalo to make him hesitate just enough to wall up some blocking around him. Buffalo is the league’s second-best rushing offense, but the Dolphins allow just 3.9 yards per rush thanks in large part to Rodriguez’s talent. Neutralizing him in the middle could make for a long day for Miami. S Michael Taaffe Taaffe is someone I really liked for Buffalo in April’s draft. He’s a hyper-athletic safety who reminded me a little bit of Cole Bishop. Like Bishop, he’s made some plays here in the early portion of his career, but he’s also been burned for some big gains. Taaffe leads the Dolphins with three interceptions, but he’s also allowed three touchdowns and a passer rating against of 100.7 this season, as opposing quarterbacks have completed 64% of their passes for a whopping 329 yards when he’s the closest man in coverage. If Buffalo can run the ball effectively, that will lead Taaffe to creep closer to the line of scrimmage to help out in run support. When that happens, the play-action pass will be on, and Buffalo could find some big plays through the air. As long as Josh Allen isn’t forcing the ball, he might be able to exploit a young player in Taaffe at the back end of Miami’s defense. If he’s not careful, though, Taaffe is more than capable of turning what looks like a big offensive play into a turnover.

title: Buffalo Bills game-day food: Frita-Cubana Meatballs
summary: How the heck long have I been doing this anyway? It doesn’t matter; the mad-kitchen scientist is back for another season of recipes to make your Buffalo Bills game days even more memorable. For those of you new to this, it’s pretty simple. We love the Bills. We love food. Every week, you’ll get a […]
full_text: How the heck long have I been doing this anyway? It doesn’t matter; the mad-kitchen scientist is back for another season of recipes to make your Buffalo Bills game days even more memorable. For those of you new to this, it’s pretty simple. We love the Bills. We love food. Every week, you’ll get a themed recipe based on the Bills and their opponent. I’ve done recipes for Miami Dolphins games lots of times and this has never come up. Is it authentic Miami? I dunno. It was good though. Frita-Cubana Meatballs How many Dolphins games have we done now? Let’s see; 2018 until now… add a playoff game, carry the one… it’s been a few. Somehow I never stumbled on frita as a food item until now. For those of you also new to the term and food, it’s a hamburger variant that mixes burger and chorizo into the patty and tops it with French fries, I wanted to make it a little more shareable and went with a meatball variation. It’ll definitely make enough to share, but maybe you won’t want to. Frita-Cubano Meatballs Makes: Enough for 4-6 people Active time: 30 min Total time: About 2 hours Ingredients 2 large eggs 1/2 red onion, minced 1/2 cup hot sauce 3 Tbsp melted butter 1 tsp salt 2 tsp black pepper 1/4 tsp cinnamon 1 lb hamburger (80/20 for the fat) 1 lb chorizo, preferably ground but you can use links (I had to, see below) 1 1/2 cups crushed potato chips Vegetable oil for cooking Essentials: Mixing bowl, high-wall fry pan, spatulas for carefully rolling and extracting meatballs, paper towels, food processor recommended Crack eggs into mixing bowl. Stir in onions, melted butter, hot sauce, salt, pepper, and cinnamon. Fold in burger and chorizo (if using links, see below). Thoroughly mix in crushed potato chips; chill in refrigerator. Add approximately one half-inch of vegetable oil to high-wall fry pan; preheat on MED/HIGH (about 6 or 7 on my stove top). Squeeze together meatballs, forming each into roughly 1-inch diameter rounds. IMPORTANT: Squeeze tightly as these tend to be a bit more fragile than traditional meatballs. Carefully place meatballs in oil, in batches; roll every few minutes to brown evenly. Continue until all sides have a crispy exterior; about 10-15 min (see picture for final color). Carefully remove from pan when fully cooked; place on a tray or large plate covered in paper towels to catch and drain excess oil. Repeat steps 7 through 8 until done. Garnish with cheese, additional hot sauce, etc. before serving. Wingin’ It tips A reminder to buy Ninja products from the link below so I can get some beer money or something maybe. If you’re looking for a good food processor that made mincing the onions trivial, mine did the trick in seconds. The same with the chorizo. On that note in particular: I ended up having to buy links, which meant removing the casing and making it mixable into the burger. I find it easiest to snip the very end of the sausage to remove the casing. And again, the processor made chopping trivial. I could have likely done the chips in here too, but didn’t think of it until after the onions and chorizo — which meant the sides had moisture on them. I also suspect the fact that I bought links contributed to some of the difficulty being cohesive. I used very firm pressure to make the meatballs, and gentle flipping until all sides were cooked thoroughly made them stable. Not enough to put on toothpicks, but enough to pick up easily. title: 5 Buffalo Bills to watch vs. the Miami Dolphins
summary: The Buffalo Bills are looking to extend their current winning streak to six games this week as they take on the Miami Dolphins, who are looking to avoid extending their own three-game losing streak. In 17 matchups with No. 17 at the helm against Miami, the Bills are 14-3. While the Dolphins did win the […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills are looking to extend their current winning streak to six games this week as they take on the Miami Dolphins, who are looking to avoid extending their own three-game losing streak. In 17 matchups with No. 17 at the helm against Miami, the Bills are 14-3. While the Dolphins did win the last time these two teams met, scoring a decisive 30-13 victory over Buffalo last November, much has changed since then. For starters, neither team’s head coach from that game is with the club, as former Buffalo head coach Sean McDermott is unemployed, and former Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel is the offensive coordinator for the 1-8 Los Angeles Chargers. Miami has torn the team down to the studs, as quarterback Tua Tagovailoa, running back De’Von Achane, and wideouts Jaylen Waddle and Tyreek Hill are either no longer with the club or injured. Buffalo, meanwhile, has started the Joe Brady era by winning eight of their new head coach’s first nine games. How can the Bills avoid dropping what should be a winnable game against a rebuilding divisional foe? It would help if their top players performed well, but with some injuries to navigate, the Bills will have some new faces stepping up this week. Here are five Bills to watch against Miami on Sunday. _____________________________________________________________________________ QB Josh Allen Allen has long dominated the Dolphins, posting video-game numbers against Miami for the whole of his career. Allen has completed 66.6% of his passes for 4,608 passing yards, 45 passing touchdowns, and 11 interceptions. On the ground, he’s run for 723 yards and five scores on 101 carries against Miami. Remember, this is across 17 games. Allen traditionally does great things against the Dolphins, and I’d expect that he’ll continue that trend this Sunday. He might not run for the kinds of yards that he did in years’ past against Miami, especially with a game coming up on Thursday night, but he will definitely be a central figure in the action. Look for the Bills to give Allen some quick-hitters early to establish a rhythm before hitting some big throws on play-action as the game progresses. TE Dawson Knox Dalton Kincaid is doubtful to play thanks to thumb and ankle injuries, and while it’s entirely possible that he suits up, he’ll likely be limited even if he does play. That means that Knox may have a chance to step up against a Miami defense that has not defended opposing tight ends well this season. George Kittle, Travis Kelce, Mason Taylor, T.J. Hockenson, Mike Gesicki, and others have either had big games or scored plenty of points—in real and fantasy football—against Miami. Knox isn’t elite, but he is a reliable target for Josh Allen as his longest-tenured pass-catcher. If Kincaid is able to go, I expect he’ll break off a big play or two, but if he can’t, expect Knox to have his best day of the season. OLB Greg Rousseau Groot is the kind of guy who can just wreck anything the Dolphins have going for them on offense. Against second-year man Kyle McCord, who will be making his second start, Rousseau presents a problem for multiple reasons. First, his length gives him the ability to block passing lanes that would otherwise be open. Second, he is shifty enough and strong enough on the edge to make McCord uncomfortable regardless of the situation. Third, the Dolphins are very weak at tackle, and having someone like Rousseau out there with Ed Oliver, Deone Walker, Bradley Chubb, T.J. Sanders, and T.J. Parker doesn’t bode well for a struggling offensive line. Austin Jackson, Miami’s starter at right tackle, is ranked No. 71 out of 72 qualifying tackles at Pro Football Focus . He’s No. 69 in pass block grade and No. 65 in run block grade. Rousseau should be excited to see Jackson across from him this week. LB Kaleb Elarms-Orr The rookie is likely to start this week with veteran Dorian Williams out due to a calf injury he suffered in last week’s win over the New York Jets. That’s a big loss for Buffalo, as Williams has been very good of late. However, the team is high on Elarms-Orr, and he has flashed some big-hitting ability early in his career. He’s appeared on just 21% of Buffalo’s defensive snaps this season, totaling 18 tackles, but he alreayd has two fumble recoveries to his name, as well. He’s struggled a bit in pass coverage, so look for Miami to try to manipulate him through motion and play-action early. Will the Bills call veteran Shaq Thompson up from the practice squad to supplement the linebacker group this week? And, if they do, will Thompson eat into Alarms-Orr’s playing time? We’ll find out on Sunday, but look for No. 52 to make some big hits this week. CB Maxwell Hairston The second-year man has looked totally lost this season, as a rookie year that flashed some potential has given way to a second season where he has lost not only a shot at a starting gig, but really any shot at playing many meaningful snaps. Rookie Davison Igbinosun has far outplayed Hairston this season, but with Christian Benford out this week, Hairston has a chance to build back some trust with the coaching staff. Miami’s passing game isn’t exactly elite—it’s not even league-average, as the Dolphins rank No. 31 in attempts, No. 29 in passing yards, and No. 29 in passing touchdowns—so this is a good time for Hairston to make a play or two. I think the ship has sailed, at least for now, where we look at Hairston as someone who should be playing when all of Buffalo’s corners are healthy; however, it would be nice for him to have a week where he looks like someone who could play in a big spot if needed. That’s a low bar to clear, but one he’s consistently knocked over throughout this season. Veteran Tre’Davious White may see time as a practice squad elevation, too. If Hairston can’t see snaps and play effectively this week, then it might be time for a bigger conversation about the former Kentucky product.

title: Discussion: Is today’s game a must win for the Panthers?
summary: It’s rare that an interconference match-up in November has enough stakes to be considered a must win, but the Carolina Panthers might find themselves in a position where that’s the case. They’re currently just 4-5, but that’s enough to lead the NFC South by a game over the Saints and Buccaneers with the Falcons just […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 20: Running back Kenyan Drake #17 of the Baltimore Ravens is tackled by defensive tackle Bravvion Roy #93 of the Carolina Panthers in the fourth quarter at M&T Bank Stadium on November 20, 2022 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Rob Carr/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s rare that an interconference match-up in November has enough stakes to be considered a must win, but the Carolina Panthers might find themselves in a position where that’s the case. They’re currently just 4-5, but that’s enough to lead the NFC South by a game over the Saints and Buccaneers with the Falcons just one extra loss behind. It’s a tightly packed race, and by rule, someone has to win the division and make the playoffs. The Panthers are coming off a key step towards winning the division with a road win over the Saints last week. Up next is the Ravens. Going into the season, this looked like a tough game, probably even penciled in as a loss for the Panthers. But now the Ravens are on their third string quarterback who they just traded for like two weeks ago. The Panthers are favorites, so they should win this game. But the question is, do they have to? Is today’s game against the Ravens a must win? MY TAKE: Yes it is. The Panthers still could win the division with a loss, but their road will be a whole lot tougher for it. After this game, the Panthers will have seven games left on their schedule. Three of those are against NFC South rivals with one game apiece. The Panthers can win all of those. But winning all of those gets them to seven wins, and seven wins seems very unlikely to make the playoffs in a 17 game schedule, no matter how bad the division is. They have to get at least one or two more wins from outside the division from here on out, and this is by far the best chance for them to do it. The rest of the Panthers non-division schedule looks like this: vs Ravens @ Vikings vs Bengals @ Steelers vs Seahawks This is definitely the Panthers’ chance to get a win, and it’s very likely it’s the only game they’ll be favored in. The Steelers are gettable, but the other three teams on this schedule have legitimate Super Bowl aspirations. It’s hard to see the Panthers stealing one of those games. The best path for the Panthers to make the playoffs is to take care of their division games and steal at least one more game outside the division. The rest of the non-divisional schedule is brutal, so that makes today a must win game, in my opinion.

summary: The Carolina Panthers have been on an odd run of injuries, poor discipline, horrible officiating, and good opponents for too long now. Injury luck, if only for the moment, seems to be a tide turning in the Panthers’ favor; discipline may yet prove to be the deciding factor in head coach Dave Canales’ tenure; and […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - NOVEMBER 20: Lamar Jackson #8 of the Baltimore Ravens shakes hands with Baker Mayfield #6 of the Carolina Panthers after an NFL football game at M&T Bank Stadium on November 20, 2022 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers have been on an odd run of injuries, poor discipline, horrible officiating, and good opponents for too long now. Injury luck, if only for the moment, seems to be a tide turning in the Panthers’ favor; discipline may yet prove to be the deciding factor in head coach Dave Canales’ tenure; and the quality of their opponent this week is certainly up for debate. Whether we’re talking Lamar Jackson or Marlon Humphrey, the Baltimore Ravens are perhaps the first team missing as much talent as the Panthers—if not more—that Carolina has seen on their schedule this season. Enter Jacoby Brissett. The spry, 33-year old, ten year veteran was acquired by the Ravens via trade on November 6th after Jackson and backup quarterback Tyler Huntley were both lost for the season after only five pass attempts against the Buffalo Bills in Week 8. Brissett started his first game just last Monday, November 16th, for the Ravens and attempted 49 passes in a three-point loss to the Los Angeles Chargers. We don’t know what we’re going to see from Brissett tomorrow. He’s with a new team, has a history of ups and downs as a starter, and is coming off of a short week of preparation. Brissett and the Ravens are a true wildcard. Maybe Will Lee III and Mike Jackson returning will be enough to iron out any concerns over what Brissett and Ravens team in disarray will bring to the field. Then again, we’re pinning a lot of hope there on a rookie corner returning from injury who has shown both promise and a penchant for his own discipline related penalties. That’s not to mention the broader penalty issues or quarterback Bryce Young’s returning lack of consistency. Maybe that’s why, at -2.5, the Panthers are favored over the Ravens in what is tied as the second narrowest spread on FanDuel this week. There are as many reasons to be optimistic about the Panthers in this and future weeks as there are reasons to keep them firmly in the “I’ll believe it when I see it” category. Meanwhile, a renewed focus on wide receivers dovetails with Humphrey’s absence in a way that hastens and increases the Panthers scoring drives. title: Reacts Results: Win and you’re in their hearts
summary: All it took is one skin-of-their-teeth win over the New Orleans Saints to end a three-game losing skid, seize first place in the NFC South, and restore some faith from fans for the 4-5 Carolina Panthers. It helps, of course, that they are facing, at home, a 4-6 Baltimore Ravens team who is on their […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 16: Jacoby Brissett #11 of the Baltimore Ravens warms up prior to the game against the Los Angeles Chargers at M&T Bank Stadium on November 16, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images All it took is one skin-of-their-teeth win over the New Orleans Saints to end a three-game losing skid, seize first place in the NFC South, and restore some faith from fans for the 4-5 Carolina Panthers. It helps, of course, that they are facing, at home, a 4-6 Baltimore Ravens team who is on their own five-game losing streak and is 1-5 in their last six games since Lamar Jackson was injured the first time for the season. This week they are giving newly acquired Jacoby Brissett his second start at quarterback for the Ravens and we’re all going to see what happens after that. Confidence rising 26% after a win in which the team arguably played a less complete game than they did in their loss to the Denver Broncos the week before has me wondering if this survey is just a lagging indicator of wins. They are the division leader with the worst record, with the NFC East leading New York Giants coming in as a close second at 5-3-1. Third place is a four way tie of 7-2 teams, including the Detroit Lions who currently sit atop a three-way 7-2 tie in the NFC North. There is no wonder we are seeing a lot of contemplation about changes to the playoff format when the Panthers are on track for a home playoff game (or whoever ‘wins’ the NFC South) and the NFC North is likely to have one or more teams with winning records miss the playoffs entirely. As for this week, most fans are unsurprisingly expecting a win. The Ravens have suffered injuries both natural and self-inflicted—looking at you, Marlon Humphrey—and are struggling to find a quarterback solution to keep their own playoff hopes on life support. The path to a wildcard berth is more open in the AFC, but extremely unlikely all the same. Have the Ravens given up as a team? Are they simply hopeless without Jackson? Are the Carolina Panthers capable of resurrecting any team’s lost pride and dignity with a surprisingly competitive game? A disciplined Panthers squad that is getting healthier are catching the ailing Ravens at the perfect time. Whether or not that is what we see on Sunday is anybody’s guess. Despite a disappointing start, Rome Odunze has shown a lot of flashes in recent weeks, particularly when it matters most. He’s helped seal the game against New England and secure an early lead against Tampa Bay – which turned out to be pretty key. While his catch rate and lack of scores are less than ideal, his yardage is there, and as he grows more comfortable, we can hope to see continued improvements from Rome. title: Bears have a chance to prove a key prediction wrong in Week 11 vs. Saints
summary: With newly acquired defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons in the fold, the Chicago Bears’ defensive outlook and philosophy have undergone a major shift for the better. That’s not just from an individual perspective, though Simmons has been great in that regard, posting three tackles for loss, two sacks, and two passes defended in his two weeks […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - NOVEMBER 15: Travis Etienne Jr. #3 of the New Orleans Saints warms up before a game against the Carolina Panthers at Caesars Superdome on November 15, 2026, in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images With newly acquired defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons in the fold, the Chicago Bears’ defensive outlook and philosophy have undergone a major shift for the better. That’s not just from an individual perspective, though Simmons has been great in that regard, posting three tackles for loss, two sacks, and two passes defended in his two weeks with the Bears. The unit as a whole has benefited from the increased double teams the All-Pro tackle has faced, allowing just 4.5 yards per play when he’s been on the field and ranking in the top 10 in EPA/play and success rate allowed since Simmons got here. But there’s one aspect in which, while improved, the Bears have remained somewhat middling at: defending the run. That’s why NFL.com ‘s Brooke Cersosimo forecasts New Orleans Saints running back Travis Etienne might be a problem for Chicago on Sunday. “Etienne returned to action last week after missing five games with a hamstring injury and looked rusty — to say the least — rushing for 14 yards on eight carries. He turns things around in dramatic fashion against the Bears on Sunday with his first 100-yard rushing performance and touchdown of the season,” Cersosimo wrote for her bold prediction for this week in NFL action. That’s definitely a choice. When healthy, Etienne is one of the better dual-threat backs in the league. But nothing about his performance in his first season with the Saints suggests he’s either of those things (142 rushing yards on 38 carries). In fact, no one in New Orleans running backs room has done much worth writing home about: through nine games, quarterback Tyler Shough leads the team with 187 rushing yards. That’s ugly. The Saints have a true running-by-committee squad, ravaged by a combination of injuries and ineffectiveness. So it’s unlikely any of them gets enough action on their own to approach 100 yards rushing unless one of them gets hot. From what we’ve seen, there’s nothing to suggest that’ll happen. Plus, if the Bears come out hot on offense and put Shough and the Saints in catch-up mode, you can forget about Etienne as a rushing threat. That, no doubt, is part of what the Bears hope to do. But it’s also important to note just how big a deal this Simmons acquisition has been for Chicago. Because yes, the Bears defense has been pretty uninspiring against the run for the past couple of years, and a player with Etienne’s skill set could definitely have given them trouble in a game like this before Simmons arrived. These days, though, the Bears have the look of a squad bent on changing that reputation (as long as Simmons stays healthy and on the field himself). The presence of an elite defensive tackle has everyone playing better, especially speedy linebacker Devin Bush. Again, there’s nothing wrong with a bold prediction or two. But let’s stash an Etienne 100-yard game in the “highly unlikely” category.

title: Chicago Bears vs. New Orleans Saints: Week 11 Players to Watch
summary: Though the Chicago Bears have won 4 of the last 5 games, including three straight prime-time matchups, the BYE week couldn’t have come at a better time as they embrace the much-needed opportunity to rest their wounded and prepare for the final stretch of the 2026 season. That starts in earnest this Sunday as Caleb […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Carl Granderson #96 and Chase Young #99 of the New Orleans Saints stand on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Though the Chicago Bears have won 4 of the last 5 games, including three straight prime-time matchups, the BYE week couldn’t have come at a better time as they embrace the much-needed opportunity to rest their wounded and prepare for the final stretch of the 2026 season. That starts in earnest this Sunday as Caleb Williams and Co. host the New Orleans Saints. A team that has struggled mightily this season despite being one game behind in the race to win the putrid NFC South. Make no mistake, this is as winnable a game as the Bears will see the rest of the season, but a conference matchup in such a tight race atop the NFC is also a must-win at this point in the season, and it also happens to be against Bears’ defensive coordinator’s former team, so there will absolutely be some added emotions this week. Either way, here are a couple Saints players to keep an eye on. Starting on offense. Offense: Jordyn Tyson, #0 – WR The number 8 overall prospect selected in the 2026 NFL and the 2nd WR taken, the former Arizona State Sun Devil has been inactive for most of the season dealing with some nagging soft-tissue injuries. While Tyson was only targeted 5 times in his first action as a pro two weeks ago against Cleveland, he led the team with 13 targets (more than doubled the next most player) last week against Carolina and converted 11 of those into receptions for 80 yards. Tyson is an explosive play-maker who might not be quite as physical after the catch but reminds me of Luther Burden III with his burst in and out of cuts and how he can make defenders miss in the open field. Tyson is the type of receiver who can give our corners fits, so I will be eager to see how Dennis Allen plans to slow him down while not losing track of the big-play weapons like Chris Olave, Barion Brown and fellow rookie Bryce Lance. With a depleted offensive line, I expect much more quick passes from QB Tyler Shough, so Tyson figures to once again receive the bulk of the targets. If Chicago can limit his YAC, they should force New Orleans to turn the ball over and score enough points on offense to put this one away. That is, if they can slow down the Saints pass rush. Defense: Carl Granderson, #96 – DE With two players in the top 5 of the current NFL sack leaders, the Saints boast as potent of a pass-rush threat as any team in the league. Carl Granderson holds the slight edge with 8.5 sacks to Chase Young’s 8.0, but both players will be key in containing Caleb Williams and forcing errant throws like we saw in Chicago’s last action against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Not only does Granderson lead the team in sacks, but he also leads the team in tackles for a loss with 10.5, and that is despite missing a game this season already. While I have the utmost confidence in Chicago’s OL and how Ben Johnson schemes up protection, fending off these pass rushers will be a primary focal point this week. As our own Mongo Peanut pointed out , Bears Left Tackle Theo Benedet will have his work cut out for him this week. If Chicago can limit their production and prevent them from making any game-wrecking plays, the Bears should march up and down the field and put up points in droves. If not, New Orleans has a chance at an upset in Week 11. What about you? Which New Orleans players figure to be most important for a Saints victory, outside of QB Tyler Shough?!

title: Caleb Williams has moved on from that 4 pick anomaly
summary: The Chicago Bears are 7-2 and coming off a much-needed bye week, which allowed them to regroup and refresh after a first half of the season in which they led the league in time of possession. They’ll also get back one of their key offensive players, running back Kyle Monangai, who hasn’t played since Week […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 8: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates a touchdown during a game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Soldier Field on November 8, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears are 7-2 and coming off a much-needed bye week, which allowed them to regroup and refresh after a first half of the season in which they led the league in time of possession. They’ll also get back one of their key offensive players, running back Kyle Monangai, who hasn’t played since Week 4. Also, wideout Luther Burden III, who exited their last game with a concussion, has cleared protocol during the bye and will be good to go this Sunday. Chicago’s bye really came at a perfect time for the team, although it also came after Caleb Williams threw four interceptions against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Caleb’s competitiveness and drive are well chronicled, so he was asked earlier this week if that performance has lingered with him at all during the bye. After breaking down the four picks as one “bad decision,” two of them “funky,” and one where the ball “popped up in the air,” he explained what stuck with him during the week. “The biggest thing is, the frustration comes from the feeling of, for me, personally, I always don’t want to let my teammates down,” Williams said from Halas Hall. “That’s always big for me. And in that situation, in those situations, I feel like I did. And so, that’s the frustrating part that lingers.” You can tell Williams is itching to get back out there and put that game behind him, but did you realize that even with those 4 interceptions, he’s still the least-intercepted quarterback in league history? Okay, technically Williams doesn’t have enough attempts to qualify for the all-time leaderboard, but his 1.36 interception percentage is lower than Aaron Rodgers’ 1.42%. Williams needs 175 more passing attempts to reach 1,500, and if he stays under Rodgers’ interception percentage mark, he’ll be the new and official number-one least-intercepted QB, per Pro Football Reference . Then again, Rodgers is still active, so he’ll have a say in the number, but regardless, Caleb is in rare air with how safe he is with the football. “I’ll move on from it,” he said about his 4 pick game anomaly. “I’ve moved on from it,” he clarified. “You know, it’s more of a how can I get better? What can I be better at? Just finding ways to be more consistent. And in those other situations where, you know, I’m not making a dumb decision like the first one. I’m trying to either get it out of bounds or, you know, anything like that — just juice it out of bounds.” The Bears host the New Orleans Saints on Sunday, and FanDuel Sportsbook has Chicago at -11.5. The Bears’ moneyline is -720, and the game’s over/under is 48.5.

title: Question of the Day: How many wins will it take to win the NFC North?
summary: The Chicago Bears sit at 7-2, but unfortunately, the Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings also sit at 7-2, making it a 3-way tie for first. The Bears currently are losing the tiebreakers to both Detroit and Minnesota, so the Bears technically sit in 3rd place in the division, with the 6-4 Packers in last. The […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 14: Head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears and Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions shake hands following the game at Ford Field on September 14, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears sit at 7-2, but unfortunately, the Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings also sit at 7-2, making it a 3-way tie for first. The Bears currently are losing the tiebreakers to both Detroit and Minnesota, so the Bears technically sit in 3rd place in the division, with the 6-4 Packers in last. The North is a gauntlet and a half and with 6 divisional games left to be played (4 featuring the Bears), it’s going to be the divisional games that are truly going to decide who is going to win the crown and have home field advantage in the playoffs through at least the first two rounds of the playoffs. Question of the Day: How many wins will it take to win the North? I think for the Bears, it’s going to come down to which teams they beat down the stretch. With 8 games to go, however unlikely, if the Bears win their 4 games out of the division and go 1-3 in the games in the division, that’s going to put them at 12 wins, but they will probably not have the tiebreaker against any of the teams in the division if that happens, which means that won’t be enough. But if the Bears go 2-2 outside of the division and 3-1 in the divisional games, that’s also a 12-5 record, but they would be in much better shape in the tiebreaker situation. Answer. With the 0-2 divisional record, even if the Bears went 3-1 in the division and finished with 12 wins, they probably wouldn’t have the tiebreaker against everyone. If the 1 loss comes to the Packers or Vikings, that team will have the tiebreaker. If Minnesota wins 1 more divisional game, they’ll most likely have the tiebreaker against the Bears. It gets tricky for Chicago and tiebreakers within the division. Unless the Bears go 4-0 in divisional games down the stretch. However, if they do that, with New Orleans and Miami on the schedule, the Bears would be looking at, most likely, at least 6 more wins, giving them 13. 13 is the number. With 3 teams at 7-2, and with how good all four teams are, I just think it’s more likely than not that one of them reaches the 13-win total. I find it hard to believe that two of them will, given they all have divisional games remaining against each other. I think one of these teams finds a way to 13, and that’s the number that wins the North. I think if the Bears or any of the other teams reach 12 wins, that will guarantee them a wild-card playoff spot. If any of them only get to 11 wins, I think that leaves them vulnerable to missing the playoffs. An 11-6 team missing the playoffs would be wild, but if the last-place team in the North finishes 11-6, and the Seahawks or Rams can get to 11-6, that means one of them is going to be sitting home in January with 11 wins but missing the playoffs. What do you say, Bears fans? Do you think they need to win 13 games to win the division, or do you think a smaller number can get it done? Or do they need to reach an even bigger total?

title: Bears Week 11 Flashbacks: Ditka’s Revenge, Butler’s Boot, Jets Shutout
summary: Climb aboard the Gridiron Time Machine as we revisit three memorable Week 11 performances from Chicago Bears history! 1.) 1985, Bears @ Cowboys: Ditka gets the last laugh November 17, 1985 | Bears win 44-0 The 1985 Chicago Bears entered Week 11 undefeated at 10-0, but their trip to Dallas carried a little extra significance […]
full_text: Chicago Bears linebacker Brian Urlacher (54) runs upfield, chased by New York Jets Brad Smith and Brandon Moore, following an interception on the goal line in the second quarter. The Bears defeated the Jets, 10-0, at Giants Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, Sunday, November 19, 2006. (Photo by Jim Prisching/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Climb aboard the Gridiron Time Machine as we revisit three memorable Week 11 performances from Chicago Bears history! 1.) 1985, Bears @ Cowboys: Ditka gets the last laugh November 17, 1985 | Bears win 44-0 The 1985 Chicago Bears entered Week 11 undefeated at 10-0, but their trip to Dallas carried a little extra significance for head coach Mike Ditka. Waiting on the opposite sideline was Tom Landry, the legendary Cowboys coach who had brought Ditka onto his coaching staff after his playing career ended. By the time the afternoon was over, Landry probably wished his former assistant had stayed home. The Bears wasted little time making their presence felt. Richard Dent intercepted a deflected Danny White pass and returned it one yard for a touchdown to open the scoring. Mike Richardson joined the fun in the second quarter, returning another interception 36 yards for a score. Chicago led 24-0 at halftime, and things weren’t about to get any better for Dallas. November 17, 1985 #Bears #Cowboys The student vs the teacher. Chicago dominates Dallas, Dent TD. 44-0 #DaBears pic.twitter.com/UYpuQHWiOC — Old Time Football 🏈 (@Ol_TimeFootball) October 30, 2022 The Bears’ defense intercepted four passes, recovered a fumble and sacked Cowboys quarterbacks six times. Dallas managed just 171 total yards, including a miserable 52 on the ground, while converting only three of its 13 third-down opportunities. Walter Payton handled business on the offensive side, rushing for 132 yards on 22 carries. Chicago finished with 216 rushing yards and 378 total yards of offense, while Kevin Butler connected on all three of his field goal attempts. The Bears scored another 20 points in the second half, including fourth-quarter touchdown runs from Calvin Thomas and Dennis Gentry, turning an already embarrassing afternoon into a historic beatdown. Chicago walked out of Texas Stadium with a 44-0 victory, improving to 11-0 and clinching the NFC Central championship. Four interceptions, two defensive touchdowns and a 44-point shutout against America’s Team. Not a bad way to remind your former boss how far you’ve come. 2.) 1990, Bears @ Broncos: Butler gets a second chance November 18, 1990 | Bears win 16-13 (OT) The Bears entered Week 11 of the 1990 season at 8-1, riding a five-game winning streak and looking like one of the best teams in the NFC. A trip to Mile High Stadium against John Elway and the Denver Broncos would prove to be anything but easy. Chicago’s offense struggled to find the end zone for much of the afternoon, settling for a pair of Kevin Butler field goals before Brad Muster finally broke through with a 10-yard touchdown run late in the third quarter. The score gave Chicago a 13-6 advantage heading into the final period. Unfortunately, Elway wasn’t finished. The Broncos quarterback scrambled nine yards for a touchdown early in the fourth quarter, tying the game at 13 and setting up a tense finish. Chicago had an opportunity to win in regulation, but Butler’s 41-yard field goal attempt struck the left upright. Not exactly the ending the Bears had in mind. Fortunately, overtime gave Butler an opportunity to make up for the miss. After the Bears got the ball back with favorable field position, Butler stepped onto the field and drilled a 44-yard field goal to secure a 16-13 victory. While Butler supplied the game-winning points, Chicago’s ground game did much of the heavy lifting. Neal Anderson rushed for 110 yards on 28 carries, helping the Bears pile up 202 rushing yards and control the football for more than 40 minutes. The defense also made life difficult for Elway, recording six sacks and forcing two turnovers while holding Denver to just 108 rushing yards. Chicago escaped Mile High Stadium with its sixth consecutive victory, improving to 9-1 on the season. A missed game-winner, an overtime opportunity and a kicker who made sure he didn’t miss twice. Sometimes all you need is a second chance. 3.) 2006, Bears @ Jets: The defense does it again November 19, 2006 | Bears win 10-0 The 2006 Chicago Bears were already 8-1 when they traveled to the Meadowlands for a Week 11 matchup with the New York Jets. They were also beginning to establish a familiar formula for winning football games. Play outstanding defense, run the football and hope Rex Grossman doesn’t make things too interesting. Against the Jets, that formula worked just fine. Neither offense managed to score in the first half, with Chicago struggling to move the football through the air and New York finding little success against Lovie Smith’s defense. Grossman completed just 11-of-22 passes for 119 yards on the afternoon, while the Bears converted only four of their 14 third-down opportunities. Fortunately, Thomas Jones was there to keep the offense moving. Jones rushed for 121 yards on 23 carries, helping Chicago accumulate 173 yards on the ground. The Bears finished with 284 total yards of offense, but points remained difficult to come by. Robbie Gould finally broke the scoreless tie with a 20-yard field goal in the third quarter, giving Chicago a 3-0 lead. Then, early in the fourth quarter, Grossman connected with Mark Bradley for a 57-yard touchdown that provided some much-needed breathing room. That was more than enough for the Bears’ defense. Chicago intercepted Jets quarterback Chad Pennington twice, with Brian Urlacher and Nathan Vasher each recording a takeaway. Pennington finished with just 162 passing yards, and New York managed only 264 total yards despite running nine more offensive plays than Chicago. The Jets also converted just six of their 17 third-down attempts as the Bears secured their second shutout of the season. Chicago walked away with a 10-0 victory, improving to 9-1 and continuing its march toward Super Bowl XLI. Ten points, 119 passing yards and another victory. Who needs an explosive offense when the other team can’t score? Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs .

title: The plays that have set the tone for the Bengals’ defensive turnaround this season
summary: It’s no exaggeration to say Dexter Lawrence’s sack against Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward, late in the fourth quarter of Week 8, saved the Bengals’ season. On a day when the Bengals gave up 36 points and 440 yards, both season-highs for opposing offenses against the Bengals, the defense stepped up when they needed to. […]
full_text: It’s no exaggeration to say Dexter Lawrence’s sack against Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward, late in the fourth quarter of Week 8, saved the Bengals’ season. On a day when the Bengals gave up 36 points and 440 yards, both season-highs for opposing offenses against the Bengals, the defense stepped up when they needed to. Lawrence’s sack knocked the Titans out of field goal range inside the final minute of regulation with the score tied 36-36, and the Bengals capitalized in overtime with Joe Burrow running in a nine-yard touchdown on the Bengals’ drive and the defense forcing a subsequent Titans four-and-out to close out the game. Since that possession punctuated by Lawrence’s sack, the Bengals’ defense has been stellar. Against the Atlanta Falcons in Madrid, where the Falcons scored 10 points on their first two drives, the Bengals kept the Falcons off the scoreboard on six of their final seven possessions. Three of those six drives ended in punts, one ended in an interception, and another ended on a missed field goal. This past Sunday against the Pittsburgh Steelers, the Bengals forced three-and-outs on the Steelers’ first three drives, forcing five punts on 10 total Steelers drives. Cincinnati held Pittsburgh to 222 total yards Sunday night, a season-low for the Bengals’ defense and just seven weeks after allowing 411 yards to the Steelers in Pittsburgh. Going into Week 11, the Bengals’ defense ranks No. 10 in scoring and No. 19 in yards allowed per game. They’re allowing just 21.4 points per game and have just one game in their four games since the bye week where they’ve allowed more than 20 points. Have there been some frustrating moments this season? Absolutely. Week 3 at Pittsburgh, Week 8 against Tennessee, and the first half at Baltimore in Week 7 were all frustrating and shades of 2024 and 2025. But there have been a lot of bright moments so far this season that have set the tone for the Bengals’ defensive turnaround. Going all the way back to Week 1, where the Bengals forced and recovered four fumbles and sacked Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield four times, there have been plays and games that have set the stage for the revived Bengals’ defense to completely flip the narrative this season both locally and nationally. Let’s take a look at those key plays and games that have set the stage for the Bengals’ defensive turnaround. Week 1 vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers: Demetrius Knight Jr. scoop-and-score With 6:29 left in the first quarter, the Bengals trailed the Buccaneers 3-0. Tampa Bay drove 56 yards in 11 plays for a field goal on their opening drive, and the Bengals answered with a three-and-out. It wasn’t a great start, especially with Mayfield and the Buccaneers’ offense going right down the field on their opening drive. But on 3rd&9 from the Buccaneers’ own 33-yard line on Tampa Bay’s second drive, Myles Murphy and Barrett Carter got to Mayfield with Murphy jarring the ball loose. Demetrius Knight Jr. scooped it up and raced 27 yards for the Bengals’ first touchdown of the season, sending The Jungle into a frenzy. Think about all three of the Bengals’ defensive players who were involved in the play. Particularly Carter and Knight, who were much maligned as rookies in 2025. But on just their second possession of this season, Carter got to Mayfield and caused a fumble that Knight recovered and ran back for a touchdown. That set the tone for both Carter and Knight that they were going to play much faster this year and much more in a flow state. Also, Murphy, who faced criticism over a lack of production for being the Bengals’ first-round pick in 2023, finished this play by forcing the fumble. For a player who the Bengals decided not to pick up his fifth-year option, that play showed that Murphy is a vital part of the Bengals’ deep wave of pass rushers. Knight’s scoop-and-score was the first of four fumbles the Bengals would force and recover on the day, and it was also their first of four sacks on Mayfield. The Bengals currently have a +3 turnover differential and 26 sacks through nine games this season. Carter has 74 tackles through nine games, and he’s on pace for 140 this season, which would easily pass his 106 from 2025. He also has five tackles for loss, compared to just one last year, and he has five passes defensed and two forced fumbles. Knight has 71 tackles and is on pace for 134 this season, easily surpassing his 106 from a year ago. He also has four tackles for loss this season, already equaling his total as a rookie. Murphy has 2.5 sacks, two tackles for loss, six quarterback hits, and a forced fumble. All three of these guys are having really good seasons. It was worth believing in them. Week 2 at Houston Texans: Dexter Lawrence stop on 4th&1 This game started as an offensive struggle on both sides. Then, though, the Texans’ offense started to find some rhythm. On just their previous drive prior to Lawrence’s 4th&1 stop, the Texans drove into the red zone. But a botched snap on a 34-yard field goal attempt denied the Texans the game’s first score. On their next drive, though, the Texans made it to the red zone again. This time, they faced a 4th&1 from the Bengals’ 18-yard line. There was 6:59 left in the second quarter, and the Bengals had managed just 35 yards on their first four drives. But this is why the Bengals traded for Dexter Lawrence. It wasn’t just to spark the defense; it was to spark the entire team. The Texans ran a handoff to David Montgomery, ironically, a player they traded for this past offseason. Lawrence shot through the middle and stuffed Montgomery for a one-yard loss. After not showing up on the stat sheet a lot in Week 1, but still making a viable impact, Lawrence’s stop on this 4th&1 was his first big-play moment with the Bengals. It was that feeling of ‘Oh, this is why the Bengals went and got him.’ The Bengals answered by driving 81 yards in seven plays with Ja’Marr Chase hauling in a sensational 32-yard touchdown to put the Bengals up 7-0, swinging all of the momentum over to their side and taking the life out of the Reliant Stadium crowd. Lawrence finished the game with three tackles and a tackle for loss, as well as a quarterback hit. The Bengals’ defense finished with four sacks and eight tackles for loss, holding the Texans to just 60 yards rushing. Montgomery finished with just 10 yards on six carries. The Bengals currently rank 21st in allowing 123.9 rushing yards per game. However, that’s down from ranking dead last in 2025, allowing 147.1 rushing yards per game. There is marked improvement through nine games for the Bengals’ run-defense, and Lawrence’s 4th&1 stop in Houston showed his value and the Bengals’ improvements in stopping the run. Lawrence currently has five sacks and nine tackles for loss through nine games, with 28 tackles, eight quarterback hits, and a fumble recovery. Week 7 at Baltimore Ravens: Jordan Battle BIG tackle-for-loss on Derrick Henry Every Bengals fan is going to remember the game in Baltimore for Joe Burrow and the Bengals’ offense exploding for 35 unanswered points in the second half, erasing a 13-0 halftime deficit for a 35-13 season-changing win. However, there’s a defensive play from midway through the third quarter that stands out as another catalyst in the Bengals’ defensive turnaround. It’s not even the stop on 4th&2 on the first play of the fourth quarter or Demetrius Knight Jr.‘s interception as the play I’m talking about. The Bengals had just scored a touchdown on their first possession of the second half, cutting the deficit to 13-7. Momentum was starting to shift. But after allowing 258 yards to the Ravens in the first half, including going 8-11 on third down in the first 30 minutes, the Bengals now needed to flip the script on defense. On 2nd&7, Derrick Henry took a handoff to the right side. Mind you, when Derrick Henry takes a handoff to the perimeter, good luck. Especially considering the Bengals’ run defense had not been good on the…

summary: For all of us who have been Cleveland Browns fans for decades (four-plus here), the honest truth is that it takes more time and energy to defend our fandom than it has often been worth on the field. That is why Browns fans have long been the greatest fanbase in the world. We’ve loved hearing […]
full_text: For all of us who have been Cleveland Browns fans for decades ( four-plus here ), the honest truth is that it takes more time and energy to defend our fandom than it has often been worth on the field . That is why Browns fans have long been the greatest fanbase in the world. We’ve loved hearing all of the stories about your fandom and what this team means to you . Now, we are excited for Sunday Night Football for the nation to learn all about what is great about Cleveland, the fans, and (finally) the team: And, now, choosing a Browns jersey is actually a tough decision, but finally a fun one. Cleveland’s roster has a number of very good young players who, from all accounts, are good people as well. Unlike in the past, when a Browns jersey would almost certainly be Joe Thomas, Joe Haden, Nick Chubb , or one of a select few historical players, fans preparing for Christmas lists and/or shopping have to be a little more particular about which player’s number they’d like to have or buy for a Cleveland fan: CB Denzel Ward – The veteran on the list, Ward is having an All-Pro season WR KC Concepcion – The rookie who battles his stutter publicly is an inspiration off the field and is playing well on it. LB Carson Schwesinger – “Captain America” was a star as a rookie and continues to play at a high level, with a high motor and all the effort any Browns fan could want from a defender. WR Denzel Boston – A big, fun-loving receiver who makes highlight plays and seems to enjoy life, often seen with a smile on his face. TE Harold Fannin Jr. – Coming out of a smaller Ohio school to become a star in Cleveland? Yeah, that is the story of a great jersey purchase. Add that to his fight-for-every-yard mentality on the field, including a few “Angry Runs” and you have the makings of a Browns fan favorite. DT Mason Graham – The question of who would replace Myles Garrett on the defensive line has started to come from the interior with Graham. The second-year pro has exploded on the field, despite an injury limiting him for a bit, and plays with passion and determination. (He’ll get a slight knock from me and many other Buckeyes for his choice of colleges, but that can always be forgiven) OT Spencer Fano – A player I would describe as equal parts serious, goofy, and hard-working, pronounced: “Fawn-O” (like a “little baby deer,” as my friend Cami Justice explained to me), Cleveland fans love players on the offensive line, so he had to be on this list. An interesting website called Jersey Advisor has taken on the task of actively helping fans choose a jersey based on a number of criteria: …a tool that scores active NFL players on how “safe” a jersey investment they are, weighing performance, tenure, durability, sportsmanship, and popularity. Constantly updating the scores, Jersey Advisor currently has Schwesinger as the safest pick among Browns fans. After the linebacker, linemen take the next three spots, with many Cleveland fans likely to disagree with one of the choices: DE Jared Verse , Graham, and Fano. The rest of the list order may not be exactly what Browns fans would expect, but the names make sense, especially for an algorithm trying to encapsulate what every roster has going on. Check out Jersey Advisor and see their thoughts on your favorite Browns players. Which jersey would you want for Christmas or would you want to buy for a Browns fan in your life?
