title: Should the Seahawks hold Quenton Nelson out of the 49ers game?
summary: Arguably, the biggest trade deadline acquisition of the 2026 season came when the Seattle Seahawks enticed the Indianapolis Colts to part with their All-World and likely future Hall of Fame LG Quenton Nelson for the measly sum of a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder. This move was supposed to be a shot in […]
full_text: Arguably, the biggest trade deadline acquisition of the 2026 season came when the Seattle Seahawks enticed the Indianapolis Colts to part with their All-World and likely future Hall of Fame LG Quenton Nelson for the measly sum of a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder . This move was supposed to be a shot in the arm for both the pass and run game, and was likely not just a rental even though Nelson is in the final year of his contract. Moving last year’s first-round pick Grey Zabel over to RG is a clear sign that Seattle views that lineup as the ideal long term scenario to build a studly OL. Unfortunately, this new lineup lasted just one game, a rare home Monday Night Football loss to the Chicago Bears 34-17. It was one of the worst games I’ve seen the Seahawks play under Mike Macdonald, and a big part of that was the offensive line struggles. Sam Darnold was sacked three times, once by new Chicago Bear Jeffrey Simmons who was a problem all night. Zabel’s struggles at RG threw some cold water on the plan. I figured there would be growing pains, so it wasn’t necessarily a surprise. The theory is that the new lineup would be able to gel over the following two games against the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders, head into the bye feeling good, and be ready for the stretch run. A sound idea, but during the week following the Bears debacle, it was announced that Nelson had aggravated a previous knee injury that he had with the Colts and needed a procedure. As I write this, Seattle is on its bye and Macdonald has characterized Nelson as “week-to-week” stating that if they had practice over the bye, Nelson would likely not be participating. Seattle’s next game is a huge division matchup in San Francisco, one they need to win to have any hope left to win the NFC West, no matter how slim the chances are. Nelson might not even be healthy enough to play, but even if he is, should the coaching staff hold him off for another week? That probably sounds like a really dumb idea and I should be tarred and feathered for even positing that question. The Seahawks traded draft capital for Nelson, he’s one of the best guards in the NFL, and they need to decide whether or not he should be extended. Plus, every game he sits out would mean just postponing the inevitability of Zabel moving back to RG. Believe me, I get all of that. Yet, maybe it’s not so bad to shift that scenario back another week? Seattle’s rushing attack has been better of late, with 150 yards or more in two of the last four games and 120+ in three of four, with the only stinker coming against Chicago…when Nelson was playing LG and Zabel at RG. Charles Cross will hopefully be back in the lineup, but backup Josh Jones might need to play RT since Abraham Lucas injured his ankle against the Raiders. Bringing Nelson back would put the starting LT and LG for the last two games at RT and RG. That kind of sounds like a disaster waiting to happen, particularly against a strong San Francisco defense. When the Seahawks lost to the 49ers in Week 5, they gave up five sacks and turned the ball over 4 times which led directly to 21 points for San Francisco. The starting OL featured Cross, Zabel, Jalen Sundell, a platoon of Christian Haynes/Beau Stephens, and Abraham Lucas. And still Seattle arguably should have won. In this important rematch, swapping Anthony Bradford and Jones in at RG and RT couldn’t perform worse than the Week 5 OL did (knock on wood). I don’t think I’d feel as confident saying that with the projected lineup if Nelson returns given the results against Chicago. Maybe letting Nelson get another week under his belt in the system wouldn’t be such a bad thing? Seattle would have the best chance short-term to get a victory in Santa Clara. Long-term, insert Nelson into the lineup for the rest of the season and work out the kinks against the ¾ of the NFC East (Dallas Cowboys, New York Giants, and Philadelphia Eagles) before the two matchups against the Los Angeles Rams. That idea might sound counterintuitive, but it could give Seattle the best chance to win as many games as possible, a necessity if they want to make the playoffs. Survive, advance, and play your best ball at the end of the season. Holding Nelson out until after the 49ers game could be the best way to achieve all of those goals and keep their dreams alive.

title: Seahawks Reacts survey results: Fans split on starting Sam Darnold over Drew Lock
summary: The Seattle Seahawks have a big decision to make at quarterback heading into their Week 12 matchup against the San Francisco 49ers. With Sam Darnold and Drew Lock both in the conversation, Seahawks fans are nearly evenly split on who should get the start. Who should start at QB against the 49ers? Sam Darnold received […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks have a big decision to make at quarterback heading into their Week 12 matchup against the San Francisco 49ers. With Sam Darnold and Drew Lock both in the conversation, Seahawks fans are nearly evenly split on who should get the start. Who should start at QB against the 49ers? Sam Darnold received 52% of the vote, narrowly edging out Drew Lock, who finished with 48%. The results reflect just how divided the fanbase is over Seattle’s quarterback situation, despite the significant statistical gap between the two signal-callers. Lock has arguably made the most of his opportunities this season. In four appearances, including three starts, he has completed 73.1% of his passes for 837 yards, seven touchdowns and no interceptions. His 125.6 passer rating is considerably higher than Darnold’s 79.5. Darnold, meanwhile, has thrown for 1,478 yards and 10 touchdowns in seven games, but also has nine interceptions while completing just 60.2% of his passes. However, the numbers don’t tell the entire story. Darnold has faced a considerably tougher schedule, going up against four of the NFL’s top 11 scoring defenses. Lock, on the other hand, has benefited from matchups against the Cardinals and Raiders, who are tied for allowing the most points per game in the league. That context makes the debate more interesting. Lock has been more efficient and has taken better care of the football, but his performances have come against significantly weaker opposition. Darnold has struggled with turnovers, yet has faced a much tougher test throughout his starts. With Seattle preparing for another divisional showdown against San Francisco, it’s no surprise that fans remain split on who gives the team the best chance to win. Here are some of your comments! The second question focused on the broader direction of the franchise, and the results were considerably less divided. Are you confident the Seahawks are headed in the right direction? Despite the uncertainty surrounding the quarterback position, 74% of Seahawks fans remain confident that the team is headed in the right direction. That’s a strong indication that, even with questions still hanging over the offense, most of the fanbase continues to believe in the overall direction of the franchise. Mike Macdonald has already made his stance clear: Sam Darnold remains Seattle’s starting quarterback when healthy. The head coach reiterated that position this week, praising Drew Lock’s performances while emphasizing his belief in what Darnold can bring to the offense. That makes the upcoming decision particularly important, as Seattle needs to establish some stability at the position heading into the second half of the season. The stakes are also getting higher. Seattle is currently in the Wild Card picture, tied with the Rams at 6-4, while still holding an outside chance of catching San Francisco in the NFC West. With the 49ers sitting at 8-1, however, the upcoming divisional matchup carries significant weight. The Seahawks can’t afford to let uncertainty at quarterback become a recurring issue as they try to keep their playoff hopes alive. Ideally, this is a decision Seattle gets right now and doesn’t have to revisit. If the quarterback debate resurfaces later in the season, it could mean the Seahawks have reached a point where their playoff chances are already considerably slimmer, leaving very little room for another adjustment. For a team still fighting for a postseason spot, finding the right answer at quarterback now could make all the difference. The contrast between the two survey results is worth noting: Seahawks fans might not agree on who should lead the offense against San Francisco, but a clear majority still believes the organization is moving in the right direction. What do you think, Seahawks fans? Should Sam Darnold or Drew Lock start against the 49ers? And are you confident Seattle is headed in the right direction? Let us know in the comments! title: Drew Lock or Sam Darnold: Who gives the Seahawks the best chance to win?
summary: The Seattle Seahawks enter their bye week facing a decision that could define the rest of their season. Sam Darnold is expected to return from injury, but Drew Lock has done more than enough to make the quarterback conversation interesting. Lock is 3-0 in games he has started and has appeared in four victories this […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks enter their bye week facing a decision that could define the rest of their season. Sam Darnold is expected to return from injury , but Drew Lock has done more than enough to make the quarterback conversation interesting. Lock is 3-0 in games he has started and has appeared in four victories this season. Across those appearances, he has completed 68 of 93 passes (73.1%) for 837 yards, seven touchdowns and zero interceptions. He has also posted a 125.6 passer rating. Darnold, meanwhile, is 2-4 in his six full starts, with 1,478 passing yards, 10 touchdowns, nine interceptions and a 79.5 passer rating. The numbers make a compelling case for Lock. But there is more to this discussion than the stat sheet. The quality of the defenses they faced, the support provided by the running game and, perhaps most importantly, the type of football Brian Fleury wants his offense to play all matter. The numbers favor Drew Lock, but context matters There is no denying that Lock has been efficient. His 73.1% completion rate, seven touchdowns and zero interceptions are impressive, especially considering he has taken five sacks for 31 yards lost. His 125.6 passer rating is also considerably higher than Darnold’s 79.5. Darnold, on the other hand, has struggled to protect the football. Nine interceptions in six full starts is a significant problem, particularly for a team that wants to build its identity around a strong defense. He has also taken 17 sacks, losing 113 yards in the process. Lock has been more efficient, more careful with the football, and better at avoiding negative plays. Still, the sample size is considerably smaller, and the circumstances surrounding their performances have been very different. The quality of competition matters The biggest argument in Darnold’s favor is the quality of the defenses he has faced. Lock’s four appearances came against the Patriots, Cardinals twice, and Raiders. Arizona and Las Vegas have been among the league’s worst scoring defenses, while New England has been closer to the middle of the pack. Darnold, meanwhile, had a much tougher stretch. His six full starts came against Washington, the Chargers, 49ers, Broncos, Chiefs, and Bears. San Francisco, Denver, Kansas City and Chicago have all presented considerably more difficult defensive challenges than the Cardinals and Raiders. That is a meaningful difference. Lock has taken advantage of favorable matchups, while Darnold has had to deal with considerably tougher defenses. This doesn’t mean Lock’s production should be dismissed. He can only play the teams on Seattle’s schedule, and he has consistently given the Seahawks a chance to win. But comparing their raw numbers without considering the quality of the defenses they faced would be unfair. The running game hasn’t provided the same support One of the biggest differences between the two quarterbacks has been the support they have received from the running game. During Drew Lock’s four victories, Seattle’s running backs (excluding quarterback rushing) produced 472 yards on the ground, averaging 118 yards per game and 4.2 yards per carry. They also scored four touchdowns. During Sam Darnold’s four losses, the running backs managed just 260 yards, averaging 65 yards per game and 3.2 yards per carry. They scored only two touchdowns. That’s a substantial difference. Lock has benefited from a ground game that has been more productive, allowing Seattle to control the pace, stay ahead of the chains and avoid putting too much pressure on its quarterback. But the quality of the defenses they faced makes this comparison even more interesting. Darnold faced run defenses that ranked, on average something near to the 12th in the NFL. His six opponents ranked second, seventh, 10th, 13th, 19th and 24th against the run. Lock’s four opponents, meanwhile, ranked an average of 25th. Their run defenses ranked 14th, 28th, 28th and 31st. In other words, Darnold faced considerably tougher run defenses and still had to deal with a running game that averaged just 65 yards per game in his four losses. Lock had a much more favorable set of matchups and received significantly better production from his running backs. Against Washington, he threw for 379 yards and four touchdowns, while the running backs combined for just 39 yards on 17 carries. He wasn’t the reason Seattle’s offense struggled in that game. He was practically the entire offense. Ultimately, the running game has been a major advantage during Lock’s victories and a significant weakness during Darnold’s losses. That context should be part of any fair evaluation of their performances. Lock’s conservative approach might fit Fleury’s offense better This might be the most important argument in favor of giving Lock the starting job. Darnold probably has a higher ceiling. When everything clicks, he can make throws and create plays that Lock might not be capable of consistently reproducing. His best football is probably better than Lock’s best football. But the other side of that argument is just as important: Darnold’s worst performances can be considerably more damaging than Lock’s. Turnovers have been a recurring problem throughout Darnold’s career. Even during his strong stretches last season, there were moments when questionable decisions threatened to undo the good things he was doing. This season, that tendency has become increasingly difficult to ignore. Lock, at least in this current season, has played a more conservative brand of football. He has taken what defenses give him, avoided forcing throws into coverage and allowed the rest of the team to do its job. That approach could be a better fit for what Brian Fleury is trying to build offensively, especially with a defense capable of keeping games competitive. The Seahawks don’t necessarily need their quarterback to win games by himself. They need someone who can avoid putting the defense in difficult situations, protect the football and take advantage of scoring opportunities. Lock has done exactly that so far. I don’t know if Lock has the talent to win the games Darnold has lost. But Darnold’s turnovers have probably made some of the games Seattle won much more difficult than they needed to be. That is an important part of this discussion, too. This decision could define Seattle’s season There is another important consideration: Seattle might not have the luxury of changing quarterbacks again. At 6-4, the Seahawks are approaching a critical stretch of their season. Their next game against the San Francisco 49ers could determine whether they remain in contention for the NFC West title. More importantly, every loss from this point forward could seriously jeopardize their chances of making the playoffs. That’s why whoever starts against San Francisco will probably remain the starter for the rest of the season, or at least for as long as Seattle still has a realistic path to the postseason. If the Seahawks find themselves needing to change quarterbacks again after that game, it will probably mean they have already lost more games and put their playoff hopes in great danger. There would be little point in continuing to experiment with the position at that stage. This is ultimately what makes the decision so important for Mike Macdonald during the bye week. He isn’t choosing a quarterback for one game. He may be choosing the player who will lead Seattle through the most important stretch of its season. Macdonald has publicly maintained that Darnold remains the team’s starting quarterback when healthy. That suggests he is still the preferred option, and it is entirely possible that his health, rather than a decision to bench him, will determine who starts against San Francisco. But Lock has made this decision much less straightforward. Seattle doesn’t necessarily need someone capable of making spectacular plays every week. It needs someone who can keep the offense functional, protect the football and avoid turning…

summary: Even if they’re not my NFL team, I enjoy following good writers from across the league. The Athletic’s Jourdan Rodrigue (on the Rams beat) and Daniel […]
full_text: MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - NOVEMBER 21: Fred Warner #54 of the San Francisco 49ers fires the team up on the field before the game against the Arizona Cardinals at Estadio Azteca on November 21, 2022 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Even if they’re not my NFL team, I enjoy following good writers from across the league. There’s some journalists out there who either write so well or offer such good analysis that they’re worth reading, just as a fan of the game and good writing. The Athletic’s Jourdan Rodrigue (on the Rams beat) and Daniel Popper(formerly of the Chargers beat) come to mind to mind. Back when I was doing research for my season preview and prediction article, I found Matthew Coller. He’s a Vikings reporter who runs a really good substack, Purple Insider. I predicted before the season that the 49ers would be 9-1 in Week 11 , based off the offensive strength of Christian McCaffrey and George Kittle being a mismatch against opposing linebackers in coverage. Here’s why I thought back then that the 49ers would beat the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City: “Meet Blake Brandel. A jack of all trades yet master of none, Brandel filled in admirably as a swing guard last year for the Vikings. That’s doable when you’re 6’6 and not good at snapping. But as the starting center facing the shorter, stronger, faster Osa Odighizuwa? ¡Dios mío! The 49ers especially need Nick Bosa and Mykel Williams playing well here, allowing Osa to focus on messing things up for Kyler Murray. This one is in the Dallas bucket of low-medium confidence, where I’m really hoping Bet #2 is going strong (or the new trade piece is fully in the groove).” Since then, Blake Brandel has exceeded expectations, playing like a top ten center who’s slightly better at pass blocking than run blocking (as the Vikings have been mostly running outside the tackles). Osa Odighizuwa has also been pretty damn good, and now he has DeForest Buckner in a tree-on-tree battle inside. They’ll be facing Kirk Cousins instead of Kyler Murray, which makes it even more important to get pressure without letting him pick the coverage apart. On the offensive side of the ball, I think I underestimated how good Mike Evans would be. He’s singular ceiling raiser whose presence makes me feel confident on every down against any team in any situation. I also overestimated his availability. The floor for the 49ers offense still lies within Christian McCaffrey and George Kittle being healthy and playing at a high level. Which brings me to why I brought up Matthew Coller. He wrote an article today about the Vikings LB Van Ginkel and his approach to forcing turnovers . “The wildest stat demonstrating that is the fact he’s entering this weekend’s massive matchup with the San Francisco 49ers with the second most sacks in the NFL (8.5) and the most coverage snaps…“[Head Coach Kevin] O’Connell explained. “He’s rerouting two separate receivers because he knows against Green Bay that’s a critical thing where their pass game has been so dynamic. He’s rerouting two separate receivers falling right into the area, the zone that he needs to be. Then he goes and hunts the football and then recovers it…” ….The Vikings put an enormous effort into taking the ball from the other team. They have forced a turnover in every game so far this season. The coach in charge of the turnover emphasis is specials teams coach Matt Daniels, who presents to the team tendencies and techniques about how the most turnovers are caused in the NFL” Meanwhile, Blake Cashman has really taken a step forward as a coverage linebacker. Everyone’s been talking about how Brock will handle the constant blitzing, but me personally, I think a bigger key will be how the 49ers offensive playmakers will deal with such good linebacker play (maybe some of the best they’ve faced all season). Finally, let’s pray that a week away from the substation means minimal injuries tonight. Vamos 49ers! Mike Evans expected to play vs. Vikings after being listed questionable “NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo revealed that Evans is set to play, while sharing a link to a video from Evans’s agent, implying his return for Sunday night.” 49ers activate CJ West off IR ahead of Week 11 game, release Brandin Cooks “San Francisco did not elevate anyone from the practice squad, as it appears as if every player on its 53-man roster is available to play against the Vikings.” Two 49ers safeties fined after win vs. Cowboys, but Malik Mustapha not punished “Sigle was fined $6,142 for what the NFL determined was a hit on a defenseless player. Sigle’s play in defense against Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb on a second-quarter incomplete pass was not penalized at the time. Neal was fined $8,639 for his fourth-quarter facemask penalty against Cowboys return specialist KaVontae Turpin. Another 49ers safety, Malik Mustapha, was not fined on a play that drew a controversial penalty for unnecessary roughness on a hit against Lamb.” In Mexico City, 49ers’ Fred Warner can represent his heritage and boost DPOY case “Juan Quiroz, Warner’s grandfather, was born in the small village of Arandas in Jalisco, Mexico, the oldest boy in a family of 11. He moved to the Los Angeles area at 16, where he met his future wife, Doris Quiroz. They married and had three children, including Laura. Juan died in a car accident when Laura was only 7. So Fred, who has Mexican and French-Canadian roots on his mother’s side and Panamanian and African American heritage from his father, never had the chance to meet his grandfather. .Yet Juan’s influence lived on through the Spanish spoken and the Mexican food shared inside Warner’s childhood home. He can still rattle off his favorite staples, from his grandmother’s eggs and tortillas every morning to wet burritos and carne asada tacos for dinner — traditions that Warner said made his Mexican background “a big part of our upbringing.”… ….Over time, Warner has worked hard to figure out the best way to knock the ball out while ensuring he still makes the tackle. He focuses on carrying his momentum through the ball carrier so even if he doesn’t get the ball out, he makes the tackle. Warner’s grandmother might argue that his penchant for Peanut Punch perfection came from his grandfather. Juan had many interests, but among them was boxing. When Warner took up boxing as an offseason training activity a few years ago, it led to Doris speaking about Juan’s boxing affinity… ….When watching film, he takes meticulous notes on everything from route combinations to running back and quarterback tendencies. Warner says school “never really clicked” for him, but he has always had a near photographic memory for X’s and O’s. Still, he likes to take his homework a step further by digging deep into analytics for nuggets that can help. Each week, Warner receives a scouting report stocked with spreadsheets on the opponent’s personnel groupings, formations and how they deploy players out of each look. The reports are so detailed that Warner might recognize a certain personnel grouping lined up a specific way and know that offense is likely to run the ball between the right guard and right tackle. Warner also studies recent trends, preferring to look at the opponent’s past four games, and tries to put himself in the shoes of the offensive coordinator. For example: Has the run game been struggling or nonexistent and the coordinator said in the media that he wants to get it going? It all goes into Warner’s planning. This routine allows Warner to avoid “paralysis analysis,” where he’s spending so much time studying that he overthinks things. It also gives him total command of the defense on game days to the point that Dallas Cowboys offensive coordinator Klayton Adams said Warner is one of the only linebackers who makes adjustments for the secondary.”

summary: The San Francisco 49ers saw two players issued fines in the aftermath of the Dallas Cowboys game last weekend as defensive backs Siran Neal and Marques Sigle were both flagged for infractions. Neal was fined $8,639 for an unnecessary roughness penalty, stemming from a punt return in the fourth quarter, where he was flagged for […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 4: Marques Sigle #36 of the San Francisco 49ers gets set during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Levi's Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers saw two players issued fines in the aftermath of the Dallas Cowboys game last weekend as defensive backs Siran Neal and Marques Sigle were both flagged for infractions. Neal was fined $8,639 for an unnecessary roughness penalty, stemming from a punt return in the fourth quarter, where he was flagged for a facemask. The punt had initially pinned Dallas inside the 20, but Neal’s penalty on the tackle gave the Cowboys field position at their 34-yard line. Dallas would end up going 10 plays for 66 yards and a touchdown, cutting the lead to 38-32. Sigle was fined $6,142 for unnecessary roughness for a hit on a defenseless player. He was not flagged on the play, which came on a third-down incompletion early in the second quarter. Dallas would punt on the next play. Those weren’t the only two fines from the game. CeeDee Lamb was fined $23,882 for an illegal use of the helmet while delivering a block on Deommodore Lenoir on George Pickens’s 39-yard touchdown in the second quarter that put the Cowboys up 16-10. There was initially a flag thrown on the play, but it was picked up. #Cowboys WR CeeDee Lamb was fined $23,882 for illegal use of the helmet on this play. There was a flag thrown that was picked up. Looks like a shoulder hit to me 🤷🏻‍♂️ pic.twitter.com/JekeV9B018 — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) November 21, 2026 On replay, it looked like Lamb delivered a hit with his shoulder to Lenoir’s shoulder on the block. He expressed frustration earlier in the week with the penalty when revealing he got fined. “I guess as a receiver, we can get hit, but can’t deliver the punishment,” Lamb said, via the Dallas News’s Joseph Hoyt. The 49ers ended up winning 46-40, and are now moving on to face the Minnesota Vikings this weekend, with kickoff set for 5:20 p.m. on Sunday night in Mexico City. Meanwhile, the Cowboys will face the Tennessee Titans at home, looking to bounce back from the loss.

To make room, they have waived wide receiver Brandin Cooks. Additionally, Cornerback Nate Hobbs has been downgraded to “out.” The Cooks waiver makes sense given that Mike […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 8: Brandin Cooks #84 of the San Francisco 49ers walks on the field during the first quarter of an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Levi's Stadium on November 8, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers made a pair of roster moves for their upcoming game against the Minnesota Vikings. They announced that they have activated defensive lineman C.J. West. To make room, they have waived wide receiver Brandin Cooks. Additionally, Cornerback Nate Hobbs has been downgraded to “out.” The Cooks waiver makes sense given that Mike Evans is expected to play and De’Zhaun Stribling could return next month. I know some may want the 49ers to put Jacob Cowing on the chopping block, but it looks like Cooks is the odd man out. The 49ers probably didn’t want to make the decision after the Vikings game, as time was running out for West’s IR designation. West’s return will also help the defensive line, which had sack issues last week against the Dallas Cowboys. Whether you think that was blown out of proportion is up to you. West started in two games before his knee injury and was largely quiet. Now that his knee is healed, hopefully he can help the 49ers generate some significant pressure. With Hobbs being out, the 49ers have until Wednesday to make a decision . If they don’t activate Hobbs by then, his season is over. As for Cooks, he will need to clear waivers and then become a free agent. The 49ers could have a handshake agreement that, once he clears waivers, they’ll pick him back up for the practice squad, where he started his brief time with the team. Given all the time spent to get him up to speed on the offense, holding onto him in some way may be a smart move.

full_text: The San Francisco 49ers should have star wide receiver Mike Evans back for Sunday night against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 11, getting their top pass-catcher back after missing the last three games with an Achilles injury. NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo revealed that Evans is set to play, while sharing a link to a video from Evans’s agent, implying his return for Sunday night. Video from Mike Evans’ agent on Instagram. The #49ers WR is set for his return against the #Vikings tomorrow. https://t.co/IWErK9UYaQ — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) November 21, 2026 Evans had been dealing with Achilles soreness for the past few weeks and finally returned to practice this week on Thursday. Now, he’ll face an elite Vikings defense that has done a great job limiting top offenses this season.

title: The Death Zone: Where the 49ers-Vikings game gets decided
summary: In Mexico City, the San Francisco 49ers play football at 7,200 feet. The thinnest air on the field, though, will be in the last 20 yards. Climbers on Everest have a name for everything above 8,000 meters: the death zone. The body can’t adjust up there. It just runs out of time and air. And […]
full_text: (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images) In Mexico City, the San Francisco 49ers play football at 7,200 feet. The thinnest air on the field, though, will be in the last 20 yards. Climbers on Everest have a name for everything above 8,000 meters: the death zone. The body can’t adjust up there. It just runs out of time and air. And when researchers went back through decades of Everest deaths, the climbers who never made it home had the same things in common. They were exhausted. They fell behind. And they reached the top too late in the day. The red zone is football’s death zone. On Sunday, it could decide the game. The 49ers have scored touchdowns on 82.8% of their red zone trips this season, 24 of 29. According to The Associated Press, that’s the best rate of any offense since 2000. Brock Purdy has thrown 13 touchdowns inside the 20 and hasn’t been picked off once. The Minnesota Vikings allow touchdowns on 25% of red zone trips, the lowest rate of any defense over that same stretch. Two records. One summit. Don’t expect a shootout. Minnesota gives up 14 points a game, and the under has hit in eight of its nine games. Nights like this, you might only get three or four real shots at the top. Every drive is an expedition. The first downs are the base camps on the way up. The offensive line are the Sherpas, carrying the load so somebody else can stand on the summit. Nobody sprints up Everest. You climb it one camp at a time, and you don’t waste a step. Climbers start their summit push in the middle of the night, before the weather turns. Kyle Shanahan does the same thing with his opening script. The 49ers have scored on their first drive in seven of nine games this season: six touchdowns and a field goal. That’s the window before Flores has seen what’s coming. Brian Flores makes those last 20 yards feel like 8,000 meters. His defense blitzes more in the red zone than anyone, 70% of the time, per Next Gen Stats, and still plays more zone down there than anyone. He sends pressure and keeps bodies behind it. When the field shrinks, there’s nowhere left for the ball to go. By my count, when Minnesota has sent five or fewer rushers to rush inside its own 20 this season, quarterbacks have gone 6-for-20 for 30 yards. No touchdowns. Four sacks. An interception. But every mountain has a route. Both red zone passing touchdowns Minnesota has allowed in my count came when Flores sent six. When everybody comes, nobody’s left in the middle. Jared Goff found Jameson Williams. Jordan Love found Christian Watson. Quick, clean, gone. For the 49ers, the middle has a name. Against that six-man pressure this season, tight ends have caught four of the eight completions that went for 15 yards or more. Climbers carry oxygen for the final push. The 49ers carry George Kittle. Every Everest team sets a turnaround time. If you’re not on the summit by then, you turn back, no matter how close you are. On the mountain, turning around is how you live. Sunday night, it’s how you lose. Three points at the end of a 12-play climb is a turnaround, and the 49ers can’t afford many. They can’t afford any misses from Eddy Piñeiro, either, and he’ll have a little more range in the thin air. So avoid what kills climbers. Don’t wear down. Don’t fall behind, because third-and-long is where Flores’ six-man pressure is at its nastiest. And don’t get there late. It’s the matchup I’ve been circling all week on the show, and it’s the one that decides the game. Everest doesn’t care how good the climb was. It only cares who reaches the top. All season, nobody has done it better than the 49ers. On Sunday, nobody makes it harder than Minnesota.

full_text: MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - NOVEMBER 21: George Kittle #85, Jimmie Ward #1, Fred Warner #54 and Alfredo Gutierrez #77 of the San Francisco 49ers head to midfield for the coin toss the game against the Arizona Cardinals at Estadio Azteca on November 21, 2022 in Mexico City, Mexico. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images How the 49ers are uniquely equipped to beat the Vikings “One way to do that is by getting all of your eligibles in a route. For the 49ers, that’s simply running their offense. Buffalo turned quick play-action and screen passes into a profit. Quick dump-offs to tight ends for eight-yard gains are big wins against this defense. To me, if you’re an EPA (big play) team, like the Packers, the Vikings are the worst possible matchup. Whereas a success-rate-driven offense, like the 49ers, can thrive against Minnesota. Love has been conditioned, by way of his offense, to hunt the big play. Brock Purdy is undoubtedly as aggressive, but there are far more built-in outs at every level in a Kyle Shanahan offense than there are in a Matt LaFleur offense. Green Bay had several plays where Dallas Turner or Andrew Van Ginkel were in a bind in coverage, but they couldn’t take advantage. Instead, Love was sacked because his eyes were downfield. Those will show up this week with Christian McCaffrey 1-on-1 in the open field, or Keenan Allen settling into the vacated area of a blitzer, or George Kittle and Deebo Samuel keeping the offense ahead of the chains on a screen pass.” Kyle Shanahan shares final updates ahead of 49ers-Vikings “I think it’s pretty easy just because of, it’s definitely easy for the coaches just because of what our schedule’s like. I think the harder time for the players is Monday and Tuesday because that’s when all their free time is, but they’re not as sick of it yet. Probably going to be real sick of it this afternoon. We’re leaving tomorrow morning, so I bet it hits them today, bet they’ll be ready to get out of here, but it’s been a great week. We haven’t felt any annoyance. Guys have been locked in and into it and it’s been good for us.” 49ers vs. Vikings: The Standard’s 5 fast predictions (paywall) “ Kawakami: 49ers 20, Vikings 17. I’d feel much more comfortable about this pick if I knew Evans was full-go, but even without that, I think this is a Purdy Baseline Game. Unless the 49ers start turning it over, he can get them to 20 or more points almost by himself against almost anybody. If the 49ers’ defense can hold Minnesota under that, they’ll get to 9-1 and on to a big home game against Seattle next weekend.” Five vital 49ers to watch vs. Vikings in Mexico City as NFC powerhouses collide “Minnesota blitzes on 78.6 percent of pass plays. That is nearly 30 percent higher than the next closest team in the NFL. But the Vikings don’t save their blitzes for just passing situations. They will test the 49ers on all downs, and San Francisco cannot afford any plays in which their offensive line is confused on their individual assignments.” The Cowboys might be ‘America’s Team.’ The 49ers aim to become the world’s team (paywall) “Offensive lineman Isaac Alarcon is from Monterrey, Mexico, while defensive tackle Sebastian Valdez’s parents were born in Mexico. He said an aunt, uncle and cousins will be at the stadium to cheer for him Sunday. “I grew up in San Diego, but I went to TJ (Tijuana) all the time,” he said. “And it just means a lot to my family and me to be able to represent my ethnicity, my culture and just show people it’s possible.” ….Their experience Down Under was so impressive that the 49ers are considering applying for marketing rights in Australia through the league’s Global Markets Program. They are also interested in expanding their footprint in Asian markets. The NFL has had to scuttle previous attempts to play games in China, but it remains on its radar, York said. He also noted the 49ers have played preseason games in Japan three times (1989, 1995 and 2002) and said, “I know Japan would like to have us back again.” “There’s some real interest in the NFL in the Philippines,” he added. “I don’t know if I can tell you that that’s the hottest next market, but we’re looking to do something in Asia.” 49ers’ Mike Evans on track to play vs. Vikings after missing past month with Achilles injury (paywall) “The 49ers will have a walk-through practice at the Air Force Academy on Saturday morning before departing for Mexico.” ‘It felt like a calling’: How 49ers’ Christian McCaffrey is fighting for veterans (paywall) “His foundation’s flagship initiative provides medical and mental-health care for Special Operations forces veterans suffering from post-traumatic stress. The program is run in conjunction with Resilience Code, whose founder, Dr. Chad Prusmack, has worked with McCaffrey for more than a decade on his athletic performance and cognitive function. McCaffrey approached Prusmack about creating comprehensive health evaluations for veterans, providing a year of no-cost personalized care. “Here I am getting the top care on planet Earth when it comes to my brain, my body, all these different images, blood work and access to treatment,” McCaffrey said. “The thought was: Why don’t we try to do as best we can to individualize plans for these men and women who have gone through so much?”

full_text: The Commanders, on their official injury report released Saturday afternoon, listed four starters as questionable to play the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday night. Center Lucas Patrick (concussion), cornerback Amik Robertson (ankle) and running backs Rachaad White (heel) and Bill Croskey-Merritt (groin) are the questionable players, though not all questionable designations are equal in this instance. Head coach Dan Quinn essentially said that Patrick would start at center despite Nick Allegretti playing well in his absence. He was also optimistic about White, stating that the veteran RB skipped Saturday’s work to quiet some soreness in his heel. While Quinn wasn’t completely direct regarding White, it sure seems like he’s going to play. Robertson, however, is truly up in the air. He suffered an ankle injury on the last play of Friday’s practice and didn’t participate on Saturday. The Commanders will see how the ailment responds between now and game time before making a call on Robertson. If he can’t go, Rasul Douglas would play a lot more, with Mike Sainristil and Fabian Moreau helping some in the slot. Croskey-Merritt was also listed as questionable to play against the Bengals, though that designation is standard among players on injured reserve in their practice windows . The verdict on Croskey-Merritt’s status will come on Monday, when he’s activated (or not). After a week of full participation, it’s fair to expect Croskey-Merritt to be available. While receiver Treylon Burks was a DNP on Friday, it was an injury management play as he works to get his foot issue right. He didn’t receive a designation and will be available to play. Despite being limited during the practice week, safety Quan Martin (shoulder) will be available to play the Bengals. full_text: Dan Quinn spoke to reporters after the Washington Commanders finished their last full practice of the week. The team hosts the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday Night Football this week, and they’re coming off a mini-bye following last week’s Thursday Night Football win over the Giants. That break was good for the team’s injury report, as some players got a little healthier. The Commanders are still dealing with several injuries, including one that happened yesterday. CB Amik Robertson was seen limping after yesterday’s practice, and Quinn said he suffered a lower leg injury on the last play of the session. They’ll work with him over the next 48 hours to determine his game status for Monday night. Quinn said it would be a combination of Trey Amos and Rasul Douglas with Mike Sainristil and Fabian Moreau also getting reps on the inside if Robertson would miss time. Bill Croskey-Merritt is set to return from injured reserve after missing the last four games with a groin injury. Quinn wasn’t ready to committ to Bill playing Monday night, but he’s trending in the right direction and itching to get back on the field. Rachaad White didn’t practice today due to heel soreness, while WR Treylon Burks was back at practice and should be good to go with his lingering foot injury. Lucas Patrick suffered a concussion two weeks ago and was replaced by Nick Allegretti vs the Giants. That was the best the line and protections have looked in a while, but Quinn said the team is going back to Lucas now that he has cleared concussion protocol. Allegretti returns to a reserve role, able to back up the three interior OL positions. The game-winning touchdown drive in the final minutes was vintage Daniels — poised under pressure, decisive, and clutch when Washington needed him most. His PFF overall grade sits ninth among all 33 qualified quarterbacks in the league, and per PFF, the Daniels-to-Antonio Williams connection carries the second-highest passer rating pairing in the NFL. That’s not a coincidence; it’s a reflection of the route-running and timing chemistry those two have built week over week. The case to force him more targets Monday night is real. Against a Bengals defense that is at its best when it can tee off on a one-dimensional offense, David Blough needs to open the full playbook. That means rolling Daniels out, letting him threaten the edge, exploiting his clean-pocket advantage — PFF ranks him second among all quarterbacks when given a clean pocket — and creating the kind of open-space plays that make the Bengals’ pass rush irrelevant. Monday Night Football on a national stage with playoff hopes on the line. This is the kind of game Jayden Daniels has been building toward all season. Blough needs to trust him, give him room to operate, and let 5 be 5. The talent is there. The moment is here. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Hogs Haven The surprising key to victory over the Bengals Where does WAS have a competitive advantage? Believe it or not, the rushing attack. The Bengals are a poor rushing team, averaging 85 yards per game (30th), while Washington averages 117 (13th). And, for all the gnashing of teeth about the state of the offensive line and the running back stable, Washington is in the top 3rd of the league in rushing yards per attempt (4.3, tied for 11th with the Colts and Jonathan Taylor), while the Bengals are 23rd with 3.9 yards/attempt. Moreover, as I showed in the previous post, rushing defense is the key weakness of the Bengals: they currently rank 20th in rush yards against but 11th on passing yards against. Why play into their hands by getting into a passing showdown when the rushing attack is there for the taking? Remember that Washington abandoned its zone-heavy rushing attack last week in favor of duo (double team blocking on the IOL) and gap, the approaches used in the prior two years. That kind of attack recognizes the limitation of Paul at LG and their Centers as zone players and takes advantage of what they do best. (The other three linemen are zone versatile.) Well, guess what? Rachaad White is a star in duo and gap. In zone, which Washington has emphasized most of the year, White’s average yards per attempt is 3.93 and his success rate is 35% – far below average numbers in the NFL. But when he plays duo, he averages an elite 5.27 YPA and has a success rate of 55%. And when he plays gap, his YPA is an excellent 4.77 and his success rate is 54%. (Data in this paragraph are from Sumer Sports.). It looks like deemphasizing zone and focusing on duo and gap blocking not only fits the OL better, those schemes far better fit their leading rusher. If I’m the OC, I plan on running White at least 18-20 times, almost all in gap and duo. That could give him alone over 100 yards rushing. Doing so will make the play action game work far more effectively, will protect Daniels, will keep the game close, and will set up the kind of passes that can win a close game. The Cincinnati Bengals nearly pulled it off. After the 2021 season, they made an improbable run to the Super Bowl before ultimately falling four points shy of upsetting the Los Angeles Rams. It was only quarterback Joe Burrow’s sophomore NFL season, which fed plenty of optimism about what they could accomplish before his big second contract hit the books. That hope wasn’t shaken when they fell to the eventual Super Bowl champion Kansas City Chiefs in the playoffs a year later. Cincinnati was viewed as a perennial contender that had plenty of financial flexibility to maximize its window. The Bengals haven’t made the postseason since. It wasn’t until this year that Cincinnati (7-2) would be regarded as a serious challenger again. The Washington Commanders (3-5-1) want to keep turning their season around when the teams meet Monday night at Northwest Stadium. The Commanders are rightfully focused on the present, not the big picture. That said, their opponent could provide some valuable long-term lessons. title: Commanders favored to win NFC East in latest fan poll – survey results
summary: So, you’re telling me there’s a chance… Here’s what Ben Standig had to say earlier this week: The 2026 NFL regular season is past the halfway point, but the finish line remains too far away to make sweeping declarations about how the NFC East race will unfold. Suggesting that the eventual division winner will have […]
full_text: So, you’re telling me there’s a chance… Here’s what Ben Standig had to say earlier this week: The 2026 NFL regular season is past the halfway point, but the finish line remains too far away to make sweeping declarations about how the NFC East race will unfold. Suggesting that the eventual division winner will have at least eight victories doesn’t seem like a stretch, in theory. There’s a solid argument that the Washington Commanders are the best all-around team among the remaining contenders. (Step aside, Eagles.) Signs of life in a wide-open race When Washington sat at 1-3 following a dismal overseas loss to Indianapolis in Week 4, talk of an NFC East title felt like pure fantasy. Yet six games later, the burgundy & gold have quietly stitched together a 3-2-1 stretch highlighted by Thursday night’s 24-21 win over the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium that has breathed a sense of renewed optimism into at least part of the fan base. Now at 3-5-1, Washington still occupies third place in the division, trailing New York by 2 games. Even so, the underlying progress is real. Quarterback Jayden Daniels engineered a clutch late drive last Thursday night — connecting with Stefon Diggs on a 32-yard touchdown with 1:05 remaining — while Washington converted 7 of 14 third downs and held New York to 4-of-12 on third down. Moreover, over the past 6 games, the Commanders have largely protected the football — carrying a +7 turnover differential on the season while leaning on young contributors like tight end Ben Sinnott, wideout Antonio Williams, and cornerbacks Trey Amos and (the not-so-young) Amik Robertson. This week’s Reacts survey In this week’s Hogs Haven Reacts survey , we asked readers two questions to gauge the community’s temperature entering Week 11. The first was our weekly benchmark: Are you confident in the overall direction of the team? This week, 46% of respondents answered “Yes,” while 54% voted “No”. That 32-point surge from last week’s 14% approval mark mirrors the 21-point jump we saw in Week 9 after Washington beat the Eagles. Nothing cures midweek angst quite like beating a division rival in prime time! Still, the fact that 54% of voters remain in the “No” camp shows that skepticism runs deep. As several commenters and fans have mentioned, Washington has yet to beat a clear playoff contender outside of Seattle in Week 3, and they let winnable games against the Colts and Giants slip away earlier in the fall. Until the Commanders can achieve sustained winning, a majority of the fan base is keeping its guard up, and the heat will stay turned up on head coach Dan Quinn and GM Adam Peters. A massive swing in the NFC East outlook Our second question asked which team respondents believe will win the NFC East division title in 2026. Despite Washington sitting behind both New York and Dallas in the standings, the results were fairly decisive: Visit our partners at FanDuel That 54% vote represents a dramatic reversal from earlier in the season, but it stems less from sudden perfection in Ashburn than from the vulnerabilities of Washington’s rivals. The Giants First, Washington owns the head-to-head tiebreaker over the Giants (5-3-1) after Thursday’s win. Second, the schedule-makers did New York no favors. Over the final 8 weeks, the Giants must run a gauntlet that includes Jacksonville, San Francisco, Seattle, and Detroit, whereas Washington gets much softer matchups against Arizona, Tennessee, and Atlanta. The Cowboys Meanwhile, Dallas (4-6) has been unable to win back-to-back games since November 28, 2025, and its defensive struggles reached a boiling point this week when head coach Brian Schottenheimer stripped first-year coordinator Christian Parker of play-calling duties in favor of senior defensive assistant Mike Pettine. To beat out Washington for the division title, the Cowboys will have to win as many times in their remaining 7 games as the Commanders win in their final 8. Don’t forget that the Commanders still have a chance to inflict a loss on the Cowboys when they meet in Landover for the final game of the regular season in Week 18. How can Washington win the division? The math is straightforward: if Washington can match the win totals of both the Giants and Cowboys, the Commanders will be the division winner! Washington holds the tiebreaker over the Giants, and, because of the Week 5 tie, matching Dallas in the win column would put Washington a half-game ahead of the silver & blue. If, for example, the Commanders can win 5 of their final 8 games to finish 8-8-1, they would be division champs if the Giants go 3-5 and the Cowboys, who have only 7 games remaining, finish out the season 4-3. Of course, with 8 weeks to go, there are sure to be a lot of twists & turns before things are decided, but the Cowboys’ games in Week 17 vs the Giants and Week 18 on the road against the Commanders could prove to be decisive in determining the ultimate division champ. Two camps in the comments Readers in the survey article comment thread broke cleanly along familiar lines. The optimistic Pollyanna camp — voiced by Savo_UK , Redskins21Life , and BillWard among others– pointed directly to the schedule imbalance. Their consensus is that if Washington takes care of business against Arizona, Tennessee, Atlanta, and Dallas (in Week 18), stealing just 1 upset against Cincinnati, Houston, Minnesota, or Jacksonville would be enough to reach 8 wins, which could be enough to claim the division in this 2026 season. The skeptical Cassandra camp — led by theFan4Life , WillThomas , and Greengmork among others — warned against mistaking a single prime-time escape against the Giants for a turnaround. They argue that Washington’s defense still struggles to generate consistent pressure, that the roster lacks the talent to beat playoff-caliber offenses, and that finishing around .500 risks trapping the franchise in draft-position purgatory without building a true contender. My take from the cheap seats As usual, I see the glass half-full. Defensively I think the Commanders defense has looked completely different since the return of Nick Cross and Trey Amos to the lineup. In the first 5 games of 2026, the Commanders surrendered an average of 29.8 points per game. Since Week 6 in San Francisco, when Amos and Cross took the field together for the first time, Washington has given up 18.5 points per game. While that stretch did include games against the struggling Eagles and last week’s road trip to New York, it also included games against the Niners and Rams. While passing yards surrendered since Week 6 are not dramatically improved (255 per game in Wks 1-5; 232 per game in Wks 6-10), the number of passing TOUCHDOWNS surrendered has changed dramatically, from 2.8 per game (14 total) in the first 5 weeks to 0.75 per game (3 total) in the four most recent games; the secondary has not allowed more than one passing touchdown in any of those contests. title: Falcons insist winning still the goal despite trading Jessie Bates III
summary: Atlanta wanted to ensure trading away Jessie Bates III didn't send the wrong message to the team.
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. -- Overcommunication. That has been the order of business over the past several days for Atlanta Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski.

 That has included one-on-one meetings with players, small-group conversations with the team's player leadership committee and full team meetings. Stefanski has wanted to make it absolutely certain that the Falcons, despite trading two starters before the NFL trade deadline earlier this week, are not in any way giving up on this season.

 "I would tell you we've got a great group of leadership on this team," Stefanski said. "I've talked to them a lot over the last few days -- like I do all the time, but in particular now. I'm very, very confident in their leadership."

 On Monday, the Falcons traded All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a 2027 second-round draft pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick. Bates, aside from being arguably the best safety in the league, was also a team captain and one of the most respected veterans in the building.

 A day later, Atlanta traded starting center Ryan Neuzil to the Baltimore Ravens for reserve guard Andrew Vorhees and a 2028 sixth-round pick. Neuzil was a Falcons success story, starting with the team as an undrafted free agent and working his way up to a starting role.

 The Falcons are 3-6. So, in that respect, it made perfect sense to get value back for two players who were set to become free agents in the offseason. With regards to Bates, a safety had not been acquired for a second-round pick since 2018. Few could blame Atlanta for making the move.

 

 "We believe the return gives us a meaningful opportunity to strengthen this roster over time," a team source said. "That does not mean Jessie stopped being an outstanding player. We are giving up something valuable and we understand that."

 On the other hand, the Falcons are in one of the most unique positions in the NFL. Their record is ugly, but they are a half-game out of first place in a weak NFC South. All four teams in the division are sitting at three wins apiece. Atlanta finishes its season playing its NFC South rivals back-to-back-to-back.

 So, there was also an argument for standing pat and making a good-faith run at the playoffs, where the Falcons have not been since 2017. Only the New York Jets have a longer drought.

 "We're still in it," quarterback Michael Penix Jr . said. "... We're so close in a lot of areas and I feel like in this organization we view that a lot. We use that a lot. We are so close.

 "I truly believe we have the team and the guys that's going to rally and flip the script because we got a lot of guys that care. Obviously, I feel like matchup wise, I feel like our team is one of the top teams in the league."

 The Falcons have shown glimpses of that, such as last month when they toppled the previously undefeated San Francisco 49ers in an impressive performance. But since then, they have fallen to the division rival Tampa Bay Buccaneers in a full-on downpour and lost to the Cincinnati Bengals in Madrid.

 

 The schedule does not get any easier. The Kansas City Chiefs will come to town Sunday. After that, the Falcons have their bye week followed by a road game against the Minnesota Vikings , a home game against the Detroit Lions and then a trip to Cleveland. Those teams have a combined 23-10 record.

 It will be up to the team's leadership to keep the players focused on the task at hand. ESPN's FPI  is giving the Falcons only a 4.5% chance of making the playoffs, but the division remains wide open. The other three teams don't have easy schedules, either.

 Left tackle Jake Matthews , the longest-tenured Falcon and the only player left from the 2016 Super Bowl team, said Atlanta had a "really good practice" Wednesday "because everyone was kind of dialed in to 'Hey, this is our objective still and we fully expect to go out and play every weekend to win.'"

 "I think [Stefanski's] message and the point was kind of driven home that there's so much still ahead of us this season," Matthews said. "We need to double down."

title: NFL Week 11 predictions: Upsets, fantasy sleepers, stat lines, TD scorers, more
summary: Eagles upsetting the Steelers? Big receiving day for Christian McCaffrey? Touchdown for Josh Downs? Let's predict 15 things for Week 11.
full_text:
Week 11 of the  2026 NFL season is underway after the Texans defeated the Colts on  Thursday night . But what will happen in the remaining 12 games? We have 15 predictions from our NFL experts.

 First, betting analyst Pamela Maldonado picks two underdogs that could win outright. Then, analytics writer Seth Walder projects stat lines for three players. Fantasy football writer Eric Moody suggests three sleepers, and analyst Matt Bowen predicts three players who will find the end zone. Finally, analyst Ben Solak lays out four wild-card predictions.

 Could the Eagles pull off an upset over the Steelers? Is 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey in for a big receiving day against the Vikings? Does Titans quarterback Cam Ward have fantasy potential against the Cowboys? Will we see another touchdown for wide receiver Josh Downs in a Chiefs uniform?

 Let's make 15 big predictions for the Sunday and Monday action.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Upset picks | Projected stat lines 
 Fantasy sleepers, surprises 
 TD scorers | Other predictions 

 
 

 Maldonado predicts two upsets 
 

 Philadelphia Eagles +4.5 (+180 moneyline) vs. Pittsburgh Steelers 

 Quarterback Aaron Rodgers hasn't given much reason to trust Pittsburgh laying points on the road Sunday . Philadelphia's specialty is playing more man coverage and sending extra rushers, both of which have bothered Rodgers in 2026. Plus, defensive tackle  Jalen Carter can attack an offensive line that just lost guard  Mason McCormick  ( ankle ).

 Eagles backup QB  Joe Milton taking sacks is the main concern for their offense, but he can still get positive yards as a scrambler. With wide receiver  DeVonta Smith  potentially returning from a hamstring injury, the Eagles have enough to win this by a field goal.

 
 

 

 Minnesota Vikings +3 (+138 moneyline) vs. San Francisco 49ers  in Mexico City 

 Minnesota's defense remains the strength in this Sunday night matchup . Coordinator Brian Flores brings pressure from different places, and 49ers QB  Brock Purdy  took five sacks against Dallas in Week 10 . The Vikings have also been excellent at forcing field goals near the end zone.

 

 Quarterback  Kirk Cousins faces a tough matchup himself in his second start for Minnesota, but he gives it a more reliable offense than before. In Mexico City, I trust the Vikings' defense to keep this tight and give Cousins a shot to win it late.

 

 Walder predicts three stat lines 
 

 George Karlaftis , Edge, Kansas City Chiefs : 2.5 sacks, 7 pressures, 31% pass rush win rate 

 It's hard to imagine a better matchup to record a sack than this. Karlaftis typically lines up opposite the left tackle, which means he'll face Arizona's  Jayden Williams -- who ranks dead last in pass block win rate at tackle but has missed the past two weeks with a knee injury -- or Williams' backup Josh Fryar .

 Karlaftis will be chasing down rookie QB  Carson Beck in his second career start -- Beck took five sacks (at over a 20% sack rate) in his debut against the Rams  -- or veteran journeyman  Josh Johnson . Plus, the Chiefs are 15.5-point favorites , so the Cardinals almost certainly will be behind and need to pass.

 
 

 Christian McCaffrey , RB, San Francisco 49ers : 9 receptions, 74 receiving yards, 1 receiving touchdown 

 I'm focusing on McCaffrey's receiving production because I think that will be the headline here. He is already an elite receiving back, but this Vikings matchup should result in heavy usage through the air.

 All running backs catch passes more frequently against zone coverage compared to man (almost twice as often), and Minnesota plays the second-highest rate of zone coverage in the league (74%). It also blitzes the most of any team, which would cause most running backs to stay in and block most of the time. But not McCaffrey, as he still runs a route 65% of the time when the opponent blitzes.

 So when Minnesota brings the heat in Mexico City, Purdy is going to be looking for his star running back ... a lot.

 

 
 

 Joe Burrow , QB, Cincinnati Bengals : 31-of-39, 378 passing yards, 3 touchdowns, 0 sacks, 91 QBR 

 I know this is chalky considering the heater Burrow is on, but I feel especially confident that he will put up numbers against the Commanders .

 Washington blitzes 42% of the time, the third-highest rate in the league, but somehow has a below average pass rush win rate. That is quite the indictment on its ability to disrupt the opposing quarterback. And it's an especially bad combination against Burrow, who is thriving even more when blitzed (86 QBR) than when not (77 QBR) in 2026.

 

 Burrow has also become quite adept at sack avoidance (4.4% sack rate), which is partially a reflection of better pass protection this season. Plus, the Commanders have the most pass-inducing defense in the league, based on NFL Next Gen Stats' opponent pass rate over expected.

 

 Moody predicts three fantasy sleepers 
 

 Ryan Flournoy , WR, Dallas Cowboys (37.8% rostered in ESPN leagues) 

 It's easy to overlook Flournoy as the Cowboys' WR3 behind CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens , but he has been productive. Over the past six games, Flournoy has averaged 5.1 targets and 13.2 fantasy points per game.

 The Titans-Cowboys matchup has one of the highest totals on the slate. And Tennessee's defense has allowed the most receptions and fantasy points per game to wide receivers this season.

 
 

 Cam Ward , QB, Tennessee Titans (26.0%) 

 Let's stick with the same game and go with Ward, who has scored at least 19 fantasy points in each of his past two games. He'll be without wide receiver  Wan'Dale Robinson  ( ankle ) but could get back rookie  Carnell Tate , who has missed the past two games due to a shoulder injury . Ward is a dual-threat quarterback with an excellent matchup against a Cowboys defense that has allowed the third-most fantasy points and third-most rushing yards per game to quarterbacks.

 

 
 

 Justice Hill , RB, Baltimore Ravens (18.7%) 

 Ravens running back  Derrick Henry has struggled recently, averaging just 3.0 yards per carry over his past five games. Hill, on the other hand, had at least eight touches and scored at least 8.0 fantasy points in each of those games, including 18.2 fantasy points against the Jaguars in Week 9 .

 
 Hill could continue to be more involved Sunday against the Panthers . Carolina has allowed the third-most fantasy points per game to running backs this season.

 

 Bowen predicts three touchdown scorers 
 

 Josh Downs , WR, Kansas City Chiefs 

 After getting traded from the Colts , Downs caught a touchdown pass in his Chiefs debut against the Falcons . He finished with 53 receiving yards on five targets, operating as an outlet from slot alignments for quarterback  Patrick Mahomes . Plus, Downs can attack the third level on seams or wheel routes.

 Downs has a great matchup in Week 11 versus a Cardinals defense that has allowed 22 touchdown passes (tied for most in the league) and plays zone coverage on 67.5% of opponent dropbacks. Chiefs coach Andy Reid will have answers to scheme open Downs for a score.

 
 

 Javonte Williams , RB, Dallas Cowboys 

 While Williams has found the end zone only once in the past three games, he has nine rushing scores on the year and at least one goal-to-go carry in nine games. I'm expecting him to cash in on a low red zone attempt Sunday against the Titans. Tennessee has allowed 10 rushing touchdowns this season, tied for the 10th most in the NFL.

 

 
 

 Courtland Sutton , WR, Denver Broncos 

 

 Let's take Sutton in a positive matchup versus the Raiders' defense . He has only two touchdown receptions this season, but he has seen seven end zone targets from quarterback Bo Nix , including one in two of his past three games. And Las Vegas has given up 22 touchdown passes in 2026, tied with the Cardinals for the most in the league.

 

 Solak makes four more predictions 
 

 The Titans will beat the Cowboys 

 I don't particularly love the Cowboys…

title: Week 11 betting preview: Analysis, best bets, TD predictions for Sunday
summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 11 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
full_text:
Week 11 of the NFL season features several games where the spread would indicate a mismatch, but this league is full of surprises. 

 Eight remaining games have teams that are favored by at least six points, and four of them are double-digit favorites. What will that mean for game bets and prop plays? We've looked at it all in hopes of trying to find the best values.

 Ben Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Seth Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Matt Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game winners from tape study and his understanding of the league. Also included are fantasy projection creator Mike Clay's top predicted anytime TD scorers.

 Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. Let's get into it.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 

 Jump to: 
 Solak's plays | Bowen's bets  | Walder's props 
 Clay's TD projections 

 

 Solak's plays 

 

 Tampa Bay Buccaneers +6 (-110) at Detroit Lions 

 It's a good spot here for the Buccaneers, who are coming off of their bye week and are one of the healthiest teams in football. It sounds like quarterback Baker Mayfield will go, but safety Antoine Winfield Jr . (ankle) isn't ready to return to action. Meanwhile, the Lions are coming off a trip to Munich and will be without star pass rusher Aidan Hutchinson on a defense that was already absent one key star in Jack Campbell . Center Cade Mays also looks like he's out for this one, and though safety Kerby Joseph might make his long-awaited return, I'm not sure how effective he'll be.

 

 I like this matchup for the Buccaneers' defense. Tampa Bay is elite against the run, and stopping Jahmyr Gibbs is the first priority when facing Detroit. Todd Bowles has also historically had success against Jared Goff . In four games against Bowles' Buccaneers over the last three seasons, Goff averages 0.08 EPA per dropback and an adjusted net yards per attempt of only 6.1. For perspective, Goff is at 0.21 EPA per dropback and 7.6 adjusted net yards per attempt for the season. The Buccaneers have the big defensive line necessary to handle this Lions front and the blitz-heavy approach to disrupt Goff in the pocket.

 I expect a low-scoring game that the Bucs try to control with their own rushing attack. This one ends on a field goal attempt.

 Minnesota Vikings +3.5 (-118) at San Francisco 49ers 

 Happy to get the hook here on a Vikings team that might be the best team in football, so long as their quarterback is not actively limiting the offense. Minnesota's defense is so exotic that it's almost worth throwing stats out the window. Brock Purdy is the league's best quarterback against the blitz by expected points and yards per attempt, but what does that really mean against a defense like Minnesota's, which blitzes in unique ways on totally different downs than all other defenses?

 

 The high-flying 49ers offense has struggled with Brian Flores' unit a couple of times -- Minnesota won 22-17 in 2023 against a 5-1 49ers team and again in 2024 in Week 2 by a final score of 23-17. Purdy is accustomed to making quick escapes against lumbering defensive linemen; the blitzers Minnesota sends tend to be better at getting him down. And because Purdy throws with so much anticipation, he's liable for a bad pick against Flores' group as well. He has taken seven sacks and thrown three picks over two games against Minnesota's defense.

 If Purdy successfully avoids those big negatives -- which I believe he can -- it's likely because the 49ers have taken a run-heavy approach on offense with a healthy smattering of quick passes. I'm not expecting huge points from San Francisco's side, while the Vikings have the potential for big offensive outputs with Kirk Cousins under center. Remember, Cousins just faced this defense a few weeks ago with the Las Vegas Raiders , and now he gets to port over all his takeaways into an entirely new offense. That feels like a big edge here.

 

 Jahmyr Gibbs rushing yards UNDER 87.5 (-111) 

 Hello, it's me, the idiot, taking a Gibbs under.

 The Buccaneers are the best run defense in football. They're allowing 3.6 yards per carry to opposing running backs and a league-low 65.9 yards per game overall. And the Buccaneers' run-heavy approach on offense should help them limit the number of possessions the Lions get.

 Given the shakiness of the Buccaneers' linebackers in coverage, I think we see a bigger day for Gibbs through the air and a quieter day on the ground.

 Ashton Jeanty receiving yards OVER 29.5 (-105) 

 Receiving backs against the Denver Broncos tend to be a good bet, as Denver's heavy dose of man coverage gives dangerous receivers out of the backfield big opportunities in space. The Raiders definitely fit into this category, as Tre Tucker , Jalen Nailor and Jack Bech are not a sufficient enough receiver room to test the Broncos' corners in coverage. Volume in the passing game will be funneled to Brock Bowers , of course, but after him, Jeanty, against linebackers Alex Singleton and Justin Strnad , is the best matchup option the Raiders have.

 Running backs are averaging 1.40 yards per route run against the Broncos this season, the seventh-highest rate among all defenses (their 8.8 yards per reception is also seventh). Jeanty saw only four targets in Fernando Mendoza 's first start, which is tied for his season low in a game. I imagine the Raiders will make a priority of getting the ball to the checkdown more frequently in Mendoza's second start, especially given the negative matchup for the wideouts in this one.

 
 Check out the latest Super Bowl odds and major NFL awards futures . 

 

 Parker Washington receptions OVER 4.5 (-101) 

 Since Brian Burns went down with a torn right ACL in Week 3, the New York Giants have the second-highest blitz rate in football (47%). That's good news for Washington, who sees a 35% target rate against the blitz this season, relative to a 26% target rate on non-blitzed dropbacks. And on the season, the Giants run the fifth-highest rate of man coverage. More good news for Washington: He has a 38% target rate against man coverage and a 20% target rate against zone coverage.

 In this particular matchup, Washington will be the primary wide receiver option for quarterback Trevor Lawrence , as he lines up most frequently in the slot. Outside cornerbacks Greg Newsome II and Deonte Banks have been a wonderful duo for the Giants, but slot corner Dru Phillips is gettable in space. I waffle on receptions and receiving yards here, as the Lawrence-Washington connections tend to be further down the field, but I think receptions is the safer play.

 Chimere Dike receiving yards UNDER 28.5 (-115) 

 Dike has run 31 and 34 routes in the past two weeks, respectively, with Carnell Tate out with a shoulder injury. But Tate was back at practice Wednesday and Thursday (limited) and could take a huge bite into Dike's snap counts moving forward. Dike averaged only 3.1 routes per game in the seven weeks Tate was healthy.

 Wan'Dale Robinson  was just placed on injured reserve, but a majority of Robinson's routes were coming from the slot, and Dike's game of straight-line speed doesn't necessarily lend itself to the slot. Dike ran eight routes from the slot last week in Robinson's absence, and backup Xavier Restrepo ran another seven. With Tate back in the starting lineup, it's likely he'll bite into some of those snaps as well.

 Even if Dike gets a bigger route share than I'm anticipating, he went over this number only once in the two weeks in which he saw 30-plus routes. As a speed threat, he does more to stretch the field and draw coverage than draw really high-value targets. I'll buy the number now with the assumption Tate plays. And even if Tate doesn't go, I'll have some outs.

 

 

 Bowen's favorite bets
